title: Loop practice runs: four shapes on the cheap tier, with notes (#178)
body:
Four Loop runs on codex/gpt-5.6-luna and agy/gemini-3.8-flash-low, each served by web.NewRuntime on a loopback port against a throwaway goal in a scratch workspace, with lap-by-lap notes, the committed run directories, the page's snapshot JSON and HTML, and a README that distills what a loop operator needs.

Runs:
- `01M2EQC626WZFR69JBN913T41M.planner-ends`
- `01M2EQK5RH2Y04HM8XPWE7P640.validation-command`
- `01M2EQFFPMHJHM9MMZMP8RGT8H.supervisor-objects`
- `01M2EQK497YCFAC0JV2K7T66WV.group-in-task`

- planner-ends: the planner dispatched three haiku tasks one at a time and ended dispatch on its own in three seconds once the workspace listing showed all three files.
- validation-command: every task carried a shell command; the workflow ran it after the worker and recorded command, exit and `passed`; two tasks, both exit 0, dispatch ended on the record.
- supervisor-objects: a supervisor on an 8s interval objected once per task and every steer landed (`landed: true`, files on disk obey); the planner never saw evidence of file contents and re-dispatched the same task until the cap.
- group-in-task: three attempts in a Group, attempt 2 killed by scope key from a second goroutine through `runtime.KillScope`; `killed` recorded, siblings finished, the task recorded all three outcomes and a winner, and the loop went on to the planner's `next: null`.

Issues filed: #192 (runlog.Read races run.jsonl), #193 (page renders values as raw JSON), #194 (backlog.md loses finished tasks), #195 (killed turn records zero usage), #196 (supervisor's last look recorded as an errored turn), #197 (no steer or killed records on the page).

Fixes #178

title: Run page and snapshot show no steer or killed records: whether a steer landed is invisible on the page
body:
Found in the loop practice runs (#178): shape 3 run `01M2EQFFPMHJHM9MMZMP8RGT8H.supervisor-objects` and shape 4 run `01M2EQK497YCFAC0JV2K7T66WV.group-in-task`.

run.jsonl records every steer and kill with what an operator wants to know:

```
{"seq":16,...,"turn":"practice.1/task.1/worker.1/turn.1","event":{"kind":"steer","landed":true,"message":"Your supervisor objects:\n\n- Every file you write ...","source":"practice.1/task.1/supervisor.1","target":"practice.1/task.1/worker.1"}}
{"seq":20,...,"scope":"practice.1/task.1/attempts.1/attempt.2","event":{"kind":"killed","by":"operator","target":"practice.1/task.1/attempts.1/attempt.2","reason":"the operator killed attempt 2 by id from a second goroutine"}}
```

**Expected:** the run page (and `GET /api/runs/{id}`, which is the same data) shows each steer on the turn it was sent to, with its source and whether it landed, and each kill on the scope or turn it hit, with who and why; #107 and #176 made those records exist so the page could show them.

**What happened:** `GET /api/runs/01M2EQFFPMHJHM9MMZMP8RGT8H.supervisor-objects` (saved as `ephemeral/attest/loop-practice/supervisor-objects/snapshot.json`, keys run/scopes/sessions/turns/turn_usage/model_calls/totals/transcripts) contains no steer record and no `landed` field at all; the only trace of the three steers is the injected user message inside the worker transcripts, whose message id happens to start with `steer.`. The shape 4 snapshot contains no `killed` record either; the kill is visible only because the scope's and turn's error text quote the `Killed` cause ("context canceled: gimble: practice.1/task.1/attempts.1/attempt.2 was killed by operator: ..."). A steer that was dropped (landed=false) would leave no trace on the page whatsoever.

Held until #173 merges if it touches the run route; filed so the practice notes can point at it.

title: The supervisor's last look ends as an errored, interrupted turn when the worker finishes
body:
Found in the loop practice runs (#178): shape 3 run `01M2EQFFPMHJHM9MMZMP8RGT8H.supervisor-objects`.

Each task ran a Codex worker (gpt-5.6-luna) with an Antigravity supervisor (gemini-3.8-flash-low) attached through `WithSupervisor(..., WithInterval(8*time.Second))`. `Generate` cancels the supervisor's look context when the worker returns (`supervise.go`: "Generate cancels and joins its supervisors before returning"), which is right; the supervisor has nothing left to look at.

**Expected:** a look cut short because the worker finished is not a failure of anything; the turn is recorded as ended without error (or not shown as a turn at all), and the page does not list it beside real failures.

**What happened:** every task's final look is a `turn_ended` record with `error: "context canceled"` and `interrupted: true`:

```
31 01:12:41.147 turn_ended practice.1/task.1/supervisor.1/turn.8 err='context canceled' interrupted=True
65 01:14:39.775 turn_ended practice.1/task.2/supervisor.1/turn.9 err='context canceled' interrupted=True
105 01:16:32.732 turn_ended practice.1/task.3/supervisor.1/turn.12 err='context canceled' interrupted=True
```

Three of the run's 29 supervisor turns are "errors" that were nothing of the kind, and the same turn shape (`error: context canceled, interrupted: true`) is what a killed turn looks like (shape 4, `attempt.2/writer.1/turn.1`), so an operator scanning for kills and failures sees the supervisor's routine wind-down among them. A `Killed` cause names who and why; the supervisor wind-down should carry its own cause ("worker finished") or end clean.

title: A killed turn records zero usage: attempt.2's three seconds of gpt-5.6-luna cost nothing on the page
body:
Found in the loop practice runs (#178): shape 4 run `01M2EQK497YCFAC0JV2K7T66WV.group-in-task`.

Three Codex attempts (gpt-5.6-luna) started at once; an operator goroutine killed attempt 2 by id three seconds in (`runtime.KillScope(run, "practice.1/task.1/attempts.1/attempt.2", "operator", ...)`). The kill worked: the `killed` record is at seq 20, the turn ended at seq 21 with `interrupted: true`, the scope ended with the `Killed` cause, and the loop went on.

**Expected:** the killed turn's usage shows what the model consumed before the kill (it had received a prompt and run at least one tool call), so the run's totals say what the run cost.

**What happened:** the snapshot's `turn_usage` for `practice.1/task.1/attempts.1/attempt.2/writer.1/turn.1` is `{"gpt-5.6-luna": {"input": 0, "cache_read": 0, "cache_write": 0, "output": 0, "reasoning": 0, "stated_cost": 0}}`, its `model_calls` entry carries one message with every field 0, and the session total for `attempt.2/writer.1` is 0 across the board. The two attempts that finished report 14609 and 5028 input tokens. The run header's totals therefore leave out one of three attempts.

Probably the Codex app-server reports token counts at the end of a turn and an interrupted turn never gets that report; if so the adapter should read the last `tokenCount` it saw when it interrupts, or the page should mark the turn's usage as unknown rather than 0. Worth deciding which before a bake-off workflow kills losers by design and every loser costs "nothing".

title: backlog.md is empty after the planner ends dispatch: finished tasks leave no record in the backlog
body:
Found in the loop practice runs (#178): shape 1 run `01M2EQC626WZFR69JBN913T41M.planner-ends` (also shapes 2 and 4).

The planner did what was asked: it planned three tasks, dispatched them one at a time, and ended dispatch when all three files existed. On each lap it returned the "full revised task list" as the planner prompt asks, and each time it dropped the task that had just been done; on its last lap it returned `{"tasks":[],"next":null}`. `Loop` writes that answer to `scopes/practice.1/backlog.md`, so after the run the file is:

```
---
{
  "goal": "...",
  "tasks": []
}
---
```

**Expected:** an operator who opens `backlog.md` after a run (or while one is going) can see what the loop has done and what is left. `go doc` says the Loop "keeps a revisable backlog in its run scope".

**What happened:** the backlog has no notion of a finished task, so the only way the planner can keep the list honest is to remove what it finished; the record of the run's work then lives only in `run.jsonl` (`planner_decision` records) and on the page. Mid-run the file is equally silent about what was done: after task 1 it held tasks 2 and 3 only.

Either a task carries a status the planner sets (done, failed, deferred) and `backlog.md` keeps every task, or `backlog.md` is documented as "what is left" and the loop writes a companion record of decisions taken; the first matches the planner prompt's "keep deferred defects visible".

title: Run page shows scope values as raw JSON text, not as the value
body:
Found in the loop practice runs (#178): shape 1 run `01M2EQC626WZFR69JBN913T41M.planner-ends`, page saved at `ephemeral/attest/loop-practice/planner-ends/page.html`. **Expected:** a scope value set with `gimble.Set(ctx, "files in the workspace", "spring.txt (72 bytes)\nsummer.txt (82 bytes)")` is shown on the run page as that text, on two lines, the way `ScopeText` renders it for the planner (a JSON string as its text, anything else as indented JSON). **What happened:** the scope's values are rendered as the raw `ValueSet.Value` JSON in a `

files in the workspace · "spring.txt (72 bytes)\nsummer.txt (82 bytes)"

task · {"name":"Create spring haiku","description":"Create `spring.txt` in the workspace. ... ``` so a string value shows with its quotes and `\n` escapes on one line, and the task record is a one-line JSON blob. A multi-line command transcript (`"$ test -f data.txt ...\nexit 0\n"` in shape 2 run `01M2EQC7S1CTSVRBX7KRR83SXN.validation-command`) is unreadable this way, and it is the record an operator wants to read first. title: runlog.Read fails at once when the run directory exists but run.jsonl is not yet written
body:
Found in the loop practice runs (#178): shape 2 run `01M2EQC7S1CTSVRBX7KRR83SXN.validation-command` and shape 4 run `01M2EQFH6EPBFAB7KVE4RW6D4P.group-in-task`.

A program that watches a run the way the page does learns the run id from the directory `gimble.Run` makes under `runs/`, then follows the log with `runlog.Read[gimble.LifecycleRecord](ctx, dir, ...)`. `ephemeral/attest/registry/main.go` and the four programs under `ephemeral/attest/loop-practice/` all do this.

**Expected:** `runlog.Read` on a run directory that exists follows `run.jsonl` from its first record, as its doc says ("replays the run log at dir and follows it until a record whose kind is complete is observed").

**What happened:** `run.go` creates the run directory before the log's first record is written. `runlog.Read` opens `run.jsonl` once (`internal/runlog/reader.go:24`) and returns the `os.Open` error when the file is not there yet. A watcher that starts between the two returns at once with ENOENT and sees nothing. In shape 2's first run the watcher printed none of its `[log]` lines; in shape 4's first run the operator goroutine that was to kill attempt 2 by id never saw `turn_started` and no kill was sent, so the run ended clean with three finished attempts. The loop-practice programs now wait for `run.jsonl` to exist before calling Read, which is the workaround.

Either `Read` waits for the file while the ctx lives (the directory is the run's promise that the log is coming), or the run writes `run.jsonl`'s first record before the directory is visible under `runs/`.

title: gimble-workflows skill and one compiling Example per shape (#177)
body:
The beta bar says an agent should write any requested workflow shape as easily as any Go program, and until now the only teaching material was `go doc` and `internal/workflows/sprint/sprints.go`. This adds the one skill an agent reads before writing a workflow, and one compiling `Example` per shape for it to copy.

## What changed

- `.agents/skills/gimble-workflows/SKILL.md`, symlinked from `.claude/skills/gimble-workflows` the way the `df-*` skills are. It says what a run is and how ids are formed; the primitives in one table (`Run`, `Scope`, `Group`, `Loop`, `NewSession`, `Generate[T]`, `Steer` with its `landed` result, `Fork`, `Set`/`SetJSON`/`ScopeText` with `Set` infallible, `WithSupervisor`/`WithInterval`, `Killed`); how an operator reaches a live run by id through `web.Runtime.Steer`, `KillScope`, and `KillTurn` (#176) and what a kill looks like from inside; the shapes with their Example names; how to run under `web.NewRuntime` and watch at `/runs/<id>`; what is under `runs/<id>/` (`run.jsonl` and its event kinds, the session transcripts, the loop backlog, the six table files, `project.jsonl`) with jq lines for prompts, cost, and kills; and the rules a workflow author meets: the validator's findings never become the goal, the judge's input differs in kind from the actor's output, an agent can repair what it is judged against, absolute workdirs in prompts and a check for writes outside them, information lands locally, plain-English prompts, cheap models for attestation, never scan from `/` or `$HOME`, nothing under `docs/`, `internal/observation/`, `web/src/`, or generated skgo files.
- `example_shapes_test.go` in the root package: the shapes, on a scripted fake harness so their output is fixed. `example_test.go`'s `Example` is the one-turn shape; `ExampleGroup` and `ExampleLoop` stay as they were.
- Nothing under `docs/`.

## The Examples

- `Example`: one turn.
- `Example_bakeOff`: fork and bake-off; a researcher reads once, two forks propose in a `Group`, a judge on another harness picks from the proposals.
- `Example_critiqueRound`: critic reads the file against the code, writer takes or rejects each finding, two rounds at most.
- `Example_supervisedWorker`: `WithSupervisor` and `WithInterval` on one turn.
- `Example_loopWithPlanner`: planner forked from the researcher, a coder per task, `Set` for the planner.
- `Example_worktreePerCandidate`: `git worktree add` per candidate, absolute path in the prompt, `git status --porcelain` in the repository afterwards (compiled, not run: needs git).
- `Example_validationCommand`: the check chosen before the coder starts, exit code as verdict, output back to the coder (compiled, not run: runs the toolchain).
- `Example_killedTurn`: an operator kills a coder's turn by id with `web.Runtime.KillTurn` mid-turn; `Generate` returns the `Killed` cause, the body re-asks the same session, the `Loop` goes on.

## Proof

`ephemeral/attest/skill/`. Issue 177 asks for a fresh Sonnet session; the Claude CLI on this machine is logged out ("OAuth session expired and could not be refreshed"), so the session ran on `codex exec` with `gpt-5.6-luna`, given only the repository and a prompt pointing at the skill, asked for "a bake-off of two Codex sessions judged by a Claude session", and told to write the file once without compiling. Its transcript shows five read commands and one write, no `go` invocation. `go build` and `go vet` of the file it wrote exit 0 and `gofmt -l` is empty on the first try; the file is committed untouched as `ephemeral/attest/skill/bakeoff/main.go`. It follows the skill: a worktree per candidate with the absolute path in the prompt, the post-Group `git status` check, a Haiku judge told to read the diffs and not the candidates' summaries, the web runtime with a port flag.

`go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -count=1 ./...` green on `origin/main` at `b7ce435`.

Fixes #177

title: just vet, test, attest; go vet in a fresh clone (#106, #112)
body:
## What changed

Adds three Justfile recipes (`vet`, `test`, `attest`) and fixes `go vet`/`go build` failing in a fresh clone before `just build` has run.

## #112: go vet in a fresh clone

The literal symptom in the issue — `web` embedding a build directory that doesn't exist before `just build` runs — was already fixed on main by PR #132, which committed `web/build/.gitkeep` so `//go:embed all:build` has something to embed. That part needed no further work.

The actual remaining blocker was two frozen historical files: `ephemeral/review/codex-loop-api/probes/main.go` and `ephemeral/review/claude-loop-api/probes/main.go`, evidence from the PR 140 Loop review (commit 482d6a4). Their fake `HarnessAdapter` implementations predate `Close` and the current `RunTurn` return type, so both files fail to compile under `go build ./...` / `go vet ./...` on a bare checkout, regardless of whether `just build` has run.

The trade: rather than porting these fake adapters forward to the current interface (which would falsify the record of what actually ran during that review), I added a `//go:build ignore` tag to each, with a comment explaining why. This keeps the files out of `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` while leaving the historical record untouched. Verified in a fresh, detached `git worktree add` of this branch: `go vet ./...` passes with no `just build` run first.

## #106: vet, test, attest

- `vet` runs `go vet ./...`.
- `test` runs `go test -count=1 ./...` then `cd web && pnpm test`.
- `attest` runs `ephemeral/attest/just-attest/main.go`, a workflow program (modeled on `ephemeral/attest/issue-149/main.go`) that touches every gimble primitive once, live, on cheap models (`gpt-5.6-luna` for Codex, `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` for Claude): a scope with data (`Set`/`ScopeText`), a schema turn (`Generate[T]` with a hand-written `Output`) and a text turn, a steer that lands and one that drops, an interrupt via plain `context.WithCancel` (confirming the same session takes a further turn afterward — not `Session.Interrupt`, which #185 deleted from the API), a fork, a loop of laps, a group of two, and a supervised turn with an objection. It uses `web.NewRuntime` on a loopback port and prints what it saw.

### What the live run showed

Run `20260913-185144.just-attest`. Every Codex-only primitive proved out live:

- scope + `Set`/`ScopeText`: printed the goal text back.
- schema turn: `note="Attestation shimmered brightly"`.
- text turn: "The attestation shimmered brightly."
- steer landed: steered mid-turn to work the word "lighthouse" in; reply came back "The weather is calm, like a lighthouse on a quiet shore." (mentions lighthouse=true).
- steer dropped: a steer sent after the turn ended was correctly reported as dropped.
- interrupt: cancelled the turn's `context.WithCancel` mid-flight (`context canceled`), then confirmed the same worker session took a further turn afterward ("still here").
- fork: forked the worker session; the fork replied confirming it had the prior conversation.
- loop of laps: planner dispatched three lap tasks against a live model (one extra round-trip because the worker second-guessed a validator and needed a follow-up lap), each lap ran its own session and wrote its result into the scope; the planner ended dispatch once both marker files existed.

The run then failed at the group step: `claude: assistant error: authentication_failed`. This environment's Claude Code CLI has an expired OAuth session (`claude auth status` reports `loggedIn: false`; a direct `claude -p` call returns "OAuth session expired and could not be refreshed"). That's a credential/environment issue, not something fixable from here — it requires an interactive browser login. Per instructions, I'm reporting this rather than faking output or working around it.

Because the group and the supervised-turn-with-objection both need a Claude session (the group's second lane, and the objection reviewer), neither could complete live in this environment. Everything that only needed Codex proved out; the two Claude-dependent primitives are wired up and ready to run once the CLI is re-authenticated, but this run could not exercise them.

Fixes #106
Fixes #112

title: Steer reports landed or dropped; Claude steer checked live (#107, #113)
body:
`HarnessAdapter.Steer` returned only an error, so `Session.Steer` could not tell when a steer raced the end of a turn inside the adapter, and the Codex adapter answered that race with a bare nil that read as landed. A steer now says whether it landed, all the way from the adapter to the lifecycle record and the caller.

## The contract change

```go
// HarnessAdapter
Steer(ctx context.Context, sessionID, message string) (landed bool, err error)

// Session
func (s *Session) Steer(ctx context.Context, message string) (landed bool, err error)
```

`landed` is false, with a nil error, when no turn was there to receive the message: none running, or the turn ended inside the harness while the steer was on its way. The error is for a harness that could not be reached.

The bool was chosen over an `ErrSteerDropped` sentinel because a dropped steer is an outcome, not a failure. At the call site `landed, err := worker.Steer(ctx, msg)` reads as two separate questions, "did it land" and "could the harness be reached", and a workflow checks `!landed` directly. A sentinel would make every caller, wrapper, and log line that treats a non-nil error as a failure wrong by default, and would need an `errors.Is` at each site to undo that.

`Session.Steer` now calls the adapter before it records anything, records the outcome on the `Steer` lifecycle event's `Landed` field (the field and the schema already existed; `go generate .` produces no diff), emits `session.inbox.delivered` or `session.inbox.cancelled` to match, and returns `landed` as a plain value. The supervisor loop discards it as before.

The adapters: Codex reports `turn/steer` failing on a turn that has since ended as dropped, and failing on a turn that is still running as the error it is. Claude reports whether the live SDK stream took the send. agy lands whenever a print process is active to interrupt and resume, and drops otherwise.

## Tests

- `TestSteerReportsLandedOrDropped` (root, fake adapter): a steer during a turn lands; a steer with no turn running drops; a steer the adapter reports dropped because the turn ended first drops rather than failing. Each asserts `Session.Steer`'s result, what the adapter received, and the `Landed` field on both `Steer` records in `run.jsonl`.
- `TestSteerWithNoTurnRunningIsDropped` (codex): the no-turn path without a daemon or a connection, and the unknown-session error. There is no in-process app-server harness in the codex tests, so the `turn/steer` race itself is not exercised below the Session level.
- `TestSteerWithNoStreamLiveIsDropped` (claude): the no-stream path without launching Claude Code.
- `TestAdapterSteerInterruptsAndResumesInsideTurn` (agy) now asserts `landed`.
- `TestAttestEventFixture` now checks the value `Session.Steer` returns as well as the records.

## The Claude live check (#113)

`ephemeral/attest/issue-113/main.go` runs one Claude worker on `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` through a six-file task with a `sleep 3` between files, watches the workdir from a second goroutine, and once the second file exists steers the turn to name the rest `moonN.txt`. It prints `Session.Steer`'s result; the run log and the workdir listing are the evidence.

It could not run: the Claude CLI on this machine is logged out. `claude -p` on haiku answers

```
Failed to authenticate: OAuth session expired and could not be refreshed
```

and the run `01M2EPJ4QQ9KX6ARF6MSYWKJFK.issue-113` (under `ephemeral/attest/issue-113/logs/`, output in `run.log`) ends its one turn after a second with `claude: assistant error: authentication_failed`. No API key or OAuth token is in the environment either. The program and that log are committed; once the CLI is logged in, `go run ./ephemeral/attest/issue-113` is the check, and #113 stays open until it has run.

The Codex live daemon was not stopped or restarted.

Fixes #107
Refs #113

title: Live run registry: Runtime.Steer, KillScope, KillTurn by id (#176)
body:
The Go half of "steer or kill any agent from the page". `web.Runtime` now knows which runs are live and can reach any of them by id, so an operator holding only a run id, a session id, a scope key, or a turn id (what the page has) can steer a session or kill a scope or a turn. The page half waits for #173.

## What changed

- `web.Runtime` keeps `running map[string]live.Controller`, filled by `Runtime.Run` for the run's duration and emptied the moment the body returns, before the logs close. Three methods on it, each an error for an unknown or finished target:
  - `func (r *Runtime) Steer(ctx context.Context, runID, sessionID, message string) error`
  - `func (r *Runtime) KillScope(runID, scopeKey, by, reason string) error`
  - `func (r *Runtime) KillTurn(runID, turnID, by, reason string) error`
- Steer records `Source: "person"` on the `Steer` record, so the log tells an operator's steer from a supervisor's. Kill records the `Killed` lifecycle event with `By` and `Reason` through the existing `cancelScope`/`cancelTurn` with a `Killed{Target, By, Reason}` cause.
- A session is found by id through the scope table: `path.Dir(sessionID)` is its scope key, and the session is in that scope's `sessions`. A session whose scope has ended is unknown.
- The test-only `CancelTurn` hook in `export_test.go` is gone; the #175 live test kills through `web.Runtime.KillTurn`, the real thing.

## The handle shape

An internal package both sides import, `internal/live`: a `Controller` interface (`Steer`, `CancelScope`, `CancelTurn`) and a `Hook` func carried in ctx (`live.WithHook`, `live.FromContext`), the same way the observation registry rides in the runtime's ctx. `gimble.Run` hands its `*run` to the hook under the run id and calls the release when the body returns. `run`'s `cancelScope`/`cancelTurn` are renamed `CancelScope`/`CancelTurn` and gain a sibling `Steer` so the unexported type satisfies the interface; `run` itself stays unexported, nothing on `Session` changes, and the root package's exported API is unchanged. This was the smallest option: no `RunOption`, no exported `Handle` type, no change to `Run`'s signature.

## Tests

- `web.TestRuntimeReachesALiveRunByID`: a run under `web.NewRuntime` with a fake adapter is steered by session id, has a turn killed by id, and has a scope killed by key from another goroutine; the run log carries the `Steer` record with `Source: "person"` and `Landed`, and both `Killed` records placed on the turn and the scope; unknown run, session, scope, and turn ids and a finished run are errors. Passes under `-race -count=5`.
- `TestLiveKillTurnByID` (#175's live test, `GIMBLE_LIVE=1`) now kills through `web.Runtime.KillTurn`.
- The #175 tests keep their coverage through the renamed methods.

## Live run

title: Infallible Set and SetJSON; the run records a panic before it escapes (#159)
body:
Set and SetJSON return nothing. Their misuses are programming errors and panic with a message naming the key and the scope, as the errors did before: a key already set in the scope (`gimble: "task" is already set in scope "delivery.1"`), a scope that has ended (`gimble: set "late" in scope "delivery.1" after it ended`), and a ctx with no scope (`gimble: set "goal": no scope in the ctx; it must come from gimble.Run`). The float64 arm is gone: nothing used it, and it was the only real marshal failure. Every Set in a workflow was wrapped in three lines of `if err != nil { return err }` that carried no information, and authors swallowed the error because it was noise; a swallowed Set silently left a value out of every later prompt. Now misuse is loud on the first run.

The runtime has a panic boundary, so the durable record is complete when the process dies. Run recovers a panic in its body, writes RunEnded with the panic and Complete, and panics again with the original value. Group.Go recovers a child's panic into an error carrying the panic and its stack; it cancels the siblings like any other child error, Wait returns it, and when it comes back as the body's result Run writes the same terminal records and panics with it. Misuse anywhere means one thing: a complete run.jsonl and a dead process. The terminal section of Run is now one function, `finish`, so the normal path and the panic path write the same records.

Every caller loses its wrapper: `internal/workflows/sprint/sprints.go` (7 calls, on top of #186), `loop.go`'s own store of the task, the tests, the examples, and the ephemeral attest and review programs, so `go build ./...` stays green. API.md's Set section says the same.

The new signatures:

```go
func Set[V ~string | ~int | ~bool | ~[]string](ctx context.Context, key string, value V)
func SetJSON[V Output](ctx context.Context, key string, value V)
```

Tests, in `issue159_test.go`:

- `TestSetMisusePanics`: the three misuses panic with the documented messages, for Set and SetJSON, and the run that hosted them still completes.
- `TestPanicInScopeBodyIsRecordedThenEscapes`: a second Set of a key inside a Scope body escapes Run as the original panic value, and run.jsonl ends with exactly one `run_ended` carrying the message and one `complete` with no recording error.
- `TestPanicInGroupChildCancelsSiblingsAndEscapesRun`: the same misuse inside a Group.Go child cancels its sibling, Wait returns an error carrying the panic text and a goroutine stack, and Run panics with it after writing the same terminal records.

`TestScopeData` keeps the happy path. `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -count=1 -race ./...` green.

Fixes #159

title: Sprint workflow: the validator informs the planner, local prompts, dry run shows every prompt (#168)
body:
The sprint workflow's validator could reshape the goal: its objections were appended to the goal and the loop run again, so each objection became a requirement. That code is gone. Each round now runs in its own scope, and what the validator did not see working is set there as scoped context, "what the validator did not see working", which the planner reads through `ScopeText` when it plans the next round. The goal in the backlog never changes. The validator's prompt is one line: "Check this repository as the Validation section below says, changing no files and committing nothing, and report what you did not see working of the goal below." It is followed by the goal, with any "Proof:" paragraph dropped, and the Validation section of docs/definition-of-done.md read from the file at run time. No done boilerplate, no filters on findings. The `review` type is now `not_seen_working`, and the task assessment uses the same words.

Prompts are plain English and what they need is local. `cmd/sprint -issue` takes a GitHub issue number or the path of a file holding the issue's text. A number is fetched with gh and written to `.gimble/issues/<n>.md` (gitignored) before any agent runs; a file is used where it is. The goal is then one line, "Read and implement the issue in <absolute path>.", and no prompt points an agent at a remote source. `-sprint` still builds a section of SPRINTS.md. Commits for an issue are titled "Issue <n>: ...".

Every Generate call's prompt and schema can be seen before it runs. `cmd/sprint -dry-run` calls no model and runs no command: a `dryRun` harness answers each turn with an example value derived from the schema (strings as "<example field>", numbers 0, the first answer to a kind of prompt filling arrays and nullables, later ones leaving them empty and null, so the loop runs one lap and ends) and prints each turn in order: session and model, the prompt, the schema, and the answer marked "example answer (no model was called)". The record of a dry run goes to a temporary directory, not the project's runs. It is a viewer, never proof. The transcript for the throwaway issue is in ephemeral/attest/issue-168/dry-run.txt, nine turns, every prompt as a value.

AGENTS.md now says to commit and push whenever something interesting has happened, and has the "Information lands locally" rule.

Tests:
- `TestDryRunShowsEveryPromptAndKeepsFindingsOutOfTheGoal`: runs the workflow dry on an issue file; every prompt is printed with its schema, the researcher, planner, and validator prompts name the issue file by absolute path, no prompt says `gh issue view`, the validator's prompt is one line with the Validation section and no done boilerplate or Proof line, the planner's backlog goal is unchanged in all three planner turns and the third carries the validator's finding as scoped context, and the repository is untouched.
- `TestWithoutProofDropsTheProofParagraph`.
- `TestRunTaskAssessesDefinitionOfDoneWithoutValidationRecipe`, updated to the `not_seen_working` field.

Live run: `20260913-184509.sprint`, log under ephemeral/attest/issue-168/ (live.log, run.jsonl, result.txt). The sprint binary from this branch ran in a throwaway copy of the tree on issue.md, a local file (no GitHub issue was filed), with Codex `gpt-5.6-luna` for the researcher, planner, and coder and Claude `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` for the validator. The researcher and coder read the issue from the absolute path in their prompts and the coder built exactly what it asked, cmd/hello with `greeting()` and a passing test, in 56s. The run ended at the validator's first turn: the Claude CLI on this machine is logged out ("OAuth session expired and could not be refreshed"; `claude auth status` reports `loggedIn: false`), so the Claude adapter returned `authentication_failed`. The validator reporting without adding requirements was therefore not seen live; a rerun once `claude` is logged in is the remaining check.

Fixes #168

title: Cancel by id with a cause; delete Session.Interrupt (#175, #165)
body:
Tyler's rule stands: cancelling the ctx is the interrupt. What was missing is that the person who wants to stop an agent usually does not hold the pointer; an operator watching the run page has ids. So the runtime now keeps the cancel funcs it already creates, reachable by id, and cancels with a cause so a workflow can tell a kill from an ordinary shutdown. `Session.Interrupt`, the second and unused way to say the same thing, is gone.

## What changed

`scope.do` and `Group` make their ctx with `context.WithCancelCause` and keep the cancel func on the scope; a normal end still calls `cancel(nil)`. The run keeps two tables: `scopes map[string]*scope`, entered in `do` (and in `Group`) and left at the start of `end`, and `turns map[string]context.CancelCauseFunc`, keyed by turn id. `Generate` gives each turn its own ctx around `RunTurn`, registered under the turn id and removed when `RunTurn` returns, so a kill by turn id ends that one turn: `Generate` returns an error whose cause is the `Killed` (`errors.As` finds it), the scope keeps running, and the workflow decides whether to re-ask. The interrupted path reads `context.Cause` of the turn's ctx instead of `ctx.Err()`, so the turn's `TurnEnded` and the returned error carry the reason; a kill reports `session.execution.interrupted` with reason `user`, like a steered stop.

`Killed{Target, By, Reason}` is one exported type in the root package that is both the cancel cause (it has an `Error` method) and the lifecycle record of the kill (it replaces the `Interrupt` lifecycle event; the schema entry moved with it under kind `killed`). Every descendant ctx reports it through `context.Cause`.

Two unexported functions on `run`, `cancelScope(key string, cause error) error` and `cancelTurn(id string, cause error) error`, cancel by id and record the `Killed` event first, placed on the scope or on the turn's scope/session/turn. An unknown or already ended id is an error. The registry issue (#176) exports them on the web runtime.

`Loop` treats a kill of a task as a failed task, not a broken loop: the task scope's own outcome becomes its `ScopeEnded` error, the planner sees a `task failed` section with the reason on its next lap, and dispatch continues. A kill of the loop scope itself reaches the task as the inherited cause and ends dispatch like any other error. `Group` treats a killed child as gone, not as an abort: its siblings run on, and `Wait` still returns the killed child's error.

For #165: `Session.Interrupt`, the adapter type assertion, and `(*adapter).Interrupt` in `codex/`, `claude/`, and `agy/` are deleted. `AgentEvent.Interrupted` stays. The one remaining caller, the issue-130 proof program under `ephemeral/research`, now cancels a per-turn ctx. Nothing under `web/src` referenced the `Interrupt` lifecycle event (the reducers only handle the `session.execution.interrupted` agent event, which is unchanged), so `web/src` is untouched, as are `internal/observation/` and the generated skgo files; only `go generate .` (the polytype directive) ran, and it changed `jsonschema_gen.go` and `jsonschema/LifecycleRecord.json` alone.

## Tests

- `TestKillScopeClosesEverySessionAndReportsTheCause`: a scope killed by key from another goroutine; both sessions inside are closed, `Scope`, both turns, and `context.Cause` of the scope's ctx all report the `Killed`, and the log has one `killed` record on the scope.
- `TestKillTurnEndsOnlyThatTurn`: one turn killed by id; that `Generate` returns the `Killed` cause, the scope's ctx is still live, the same session completes a second turn, `TurnEnded` for turn 1 is interrupted with the reason and turn 2 is clean, the `killed` record is placed on the turn, and an unknown turn id is an error.
- `TestGroupKilledChildLeavesItsSiblingsRunning`: a `Group` of three with one child killed; the other two are still inside `RunTurn` after the kill and finish, and `Wait` returns the killed child's error.
- `TestLoopKilledTaskIsAFailedTaskNotABrokenLoop`: a killed task; `Loop.Err` is nil, a second lap runs, the planner's next prompt carries `task failed` with the reason, and the task's `ScopeEnded` records it.
- `TestCancelledTurnLeavesTheSessionUsable` (#165): a turn cancelled through its own ctx, then the same `Session` runs another turn successfully.

All five pass repeatedly under `-race`. `go build`, `go vet`, and `go test -count=1` are green for every package except `ephemeral/review/*/probes`, which already fail to compile at `origin/main` (their fakes predate `HarnessAdapter.Close`) and are not touched here.

## Live check

`TestLiveKillTurnByID` (`GIMBLE_LIVE=1 go test . -run TestLiveKillTurnByID -v`) ran one real Codex session on `gpt-5.6-luna` against the machine's shared app-server daemon: a long first turn (count to 400) was killed by id from a second goroutine 4.0 s in, ended with the `Killed` cause, the scope stayed live, and the same session completed a second turn on the same thread 2.5 s later (20224 cached tokens read). Run `20260913-184217.cancel-by-id`; its log is committed under `ephemeral/attest/cancel-by-id/logs/`: the `killed` record sits on `lap.1/worker.1/turn.1` with `by: attest`, `turn_ended` for turn 1 is `interrupted: true` with the reason, the session log has `session.execution.interrupted` with reason `user`, and turn 2 is clean.

The live check is a test rather than a `main.go` under `ephemeral/attest` because `cancelTurn` is unexported by the issue's own design until #176, so no `main` package can reach it; `export_test.go` exposes it to the external test package, which is where the `codex` import has to live to avoid a cycle.

Fixes #175
Fixes #165

title: Run ids from ulid; one seq for project.jsonl (#111, #118)
body:
Run ids were `YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.<name>` in `run.go`, colliding at `os.Mkdir` when two runs of the same name in one project started within the same second. `Run` now mints the id with `oklog/ulid`'s `Make()` (unique and monotonic within a process, no config needed) and keeps the workflow name in the directory as `<ulid>.<name>`, so the runs folder stays human-readable. No other code parses the old timestamp-shaped id: the run directory name is opaque everywhere else (the web run route, `internal/observation`, `internal/runlog`), so nothing else needed to change.

`Run` also opens its own `eventWriter` for the project-wide `<project>/project.jsonl`, and each writer's `seq` counter starts at 0, so two runs active at once in one project wrote overlapping `seq` values to that shared file. Of the two options in the issue, I dropped `Seq` from project-level records rather than adding a shared-writer registry: it needed a one-line signature change (`writeLifecycle` takes a `withSeq bool`) instead of new package-level state, refcounting, or a registry lifecycle to get wrong. `run.jsonl` keeps its real, gap-free `Seq` untouched, since each run still owns exactly one writer for its own log; `project.jsonl` records now always carry `Seq: 0`, documented on `LifecycleRecord` and at the `writeLifecycle` call sites as: order `project.jsonl` by `Time` instead.

Tests added:
- `TestIssue118ConcurrentRunsShareProjectLog` (`issue118_test.go`) runs two `Run`s of one project through a `sync.WaitGroup` barrier so both are genuinely live at the same time (neither returns until both have started), then reads `project.jsonl` back and asserts every record parses and validates against its schema, every record carries `Seq == 0`, and the two runs' start/end spans actually overlap in time — the exact scenario that used to produce colliding `seq` values. Passes under `-race` across repeated runs.
- Updated `TestRunLogCanBeRead` for the new `writeLifecycle` signature.

`go generate ./...` was re-run for `LifecycleRecord`'s updated doc comment, updating only `jsonschema/LifecycleRecord.json[.sum]`'s description string.

`go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -count=1 ./...` are green.

Fixes #111
Fixes #118

title: Codex: raise the descriptor limit before starting the shared daemon (#163)
body:
## What changed and why

When `connect()` (codex/rpc.go) finds no `codex app-server` daemon running and starts one, the daemon inherited whatever soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` the login shell handed this Gimble process — 256 by default on macOS. Go raises its own soft limit at process startup but deliberately hands children the *original* value (see `runtime/rlimit.go`), so a daemon Gimble itself starts got the low ceiling regardless of the shell's own configuration. Each loaded thread costs the daemon about 12 descriptors (MCP child pipes); a wide `Group` of parallel Codex sessions can approach or exceed 256, and the daemon logged 413 "Too many open files" errors on 2026-09-12 doing exactly that (`ephemeral/attest/codex-daemon/proof.txt`).

`raiseFileDescriptorLimit` (new file `codex/rlimit_unix.go`, build-tagged `unix` so it compiles only where `RLIMIT_NOFILE` exists) runs immediately before `codex app-server daemon start` and calls `syscall.Setrlimit` to raise this process's own soft limit — the raise that then carries over to the daemon this process execs. The target is the hard limit, capped at a sane ceiling (`darwinOpenMax = 65536`) rather than used raw: on this machine `Getrlimit` reports the hard limit as `RLIM_INFINITY` (observed as `math.MaxInt64`), and `Setrlimit` does *not* reject that sentinel — it happily sets the soft limit to literal infinity, which is its own hazard (fd-table-sized allocations, `select`'s `FD_SETSIZE` bitmap). The cap is applied before calling `Setrlimit`, not only as a fallback after a rejection. It never returns an error: a daemon that starts at the original, smaller limit is still better than one Gimble refused to start over a housekeeping call. A daemon already running is completely untouched — this only runs on the "start a new daemon" branch. Windows/plan9/wasm get a no-op stub (`codex/rlimit_other.go`).

The operator lever for the other path — a daemon started by Codex Desktop's SSH bootstrap, which inherits the login shell's limit and which Gimble cannot reach — is documented in the `codex` package doc comment (`codex/codex.go`): a `ulimit -n 65536` in `~/.zshenv` covers it on the daemon's next start.

## Test

`codex/rlimit_unix_test.go`'s `TestConnectRaisesTheDescriptorLimitBeforeStartingTheDaemon` follows the fake-`codex`-on-`PATH` pattern in `codex/codex_test.go`'s `TestCloseNeverStartsAStoppedDaemon`. It lowers this test process's own soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` to 200 (restored in `t.Cleanup`), then calls `connect(ctx, true)` against a fake `codex` that reports the daemon stopped and, on `daemon start`, records its own `ulimit -n` to a file. The recorded value (65536 on this machine, the capped ceiling) must exceed the pre-raise floor of 200; `connect`'s subsequent websocket dial to a nonexistent socket fails fast afterward, which the test ignores — it only needs the recorded value, not a working daemon.

## Live observation

A `codex app-server` daemon was already running on this machine throughout this work (pid 1516, started earlier by Codex Desktop's SSH bootstrap — its command line carries `CODEX_SSH_SKIP_APP_SERVER_BOOT`/`SSH_AUTH_SOCK` forwarding, the exact path this PR's change has no lever over). Per the issue and house rules, that daemon was never stopped or restarted to engineer a "no daemon running" condition; the "Gimble starts a fresh daemon and a wide `Group` doesn't overflow it" scenario was not exercised live on this machine for that reason. What was observed instead, without touching the daemon:

- `lsof -p 1516 | wc -l` = 120 open descriptors.
- `launchctl limit maxfiles` = soft 256 / hard unlimited (the system-wide default policy; the daemon's own per-process soft limit could not be queried without root — `ps -o lim` reports the memory limit, not `RLIMIT_NOFILE`, and `launchctl procinfo` requires root, which was not available in this session).
- `grep -c "Too many open files" ~/.codex/app-server-control/app-server.log` = 0 (no such errors logged for this daemon instance so far).

The fake-daemon unit test above is the acceptance-item proof that a daemon Gimble itself starts inherits the raised limit; the live half of the issue's acceptance criterion (`lsof` climbing past 256 during a wide `Group` without "Too many open files") did not run because no daemon-start opportunity existed on this shared machine during this work.

Fixes #163

title: The run store: seven tables of facts, six files, no checkpoint
body:
Replaces the improvised `observation.json` and `checkpoint.go` with a deliberate file-based run store, per `docs/sprints/RUN-STORE.md`.

**The store.** Seven tables of facts as Go maps in `internal/observation` (run, scope with values and decisions, session, turn, turn_usage, model_call) and six JSON array files under `runs/<id>/`, rewritten atomically under the store lock once per accepted record. Per-scope and per-session totals are summed in Go from `turn_usage` by prefix containment and pushed as a `totals` frame; the browser sums nothing and folds no lifecycle. A turn is charged to the scope it ran in, not the scope its session was created in.

**Reading a finished run.** The six files are the data model and Gimble reads them: opening a run loads the tables into the maps and reads the session logs for transcripts only, mutating none of the fact maps. The lifecycle log is replayed, and the six files written, only when a table file is missing, which is how runs recorded before this change (the saved issue-149 run) get their tables.

**Page.** `snapshot`, `row`, `totals`, `event` frames; the `scopeUsage` remote query and the browser usage fold are deleted; header, scope list, session cards, and transcripts unchanged.

**Proof.** `ephemeral/attest/run-store/result.md`: two cheap-tier live runs (Codex luna, Gemini flash; the Claude leg ran on Codex because the CLI is logged out), every page number equal to the jq sum over `turns.json` and `turn_usage.json` and to the `turn_ended` records; the page rising on one open headless-Chromium connection with no reload; the binary reopening the run from its tables with file mtimes unchanged; the issue-149 logs rebuilding to the registry test's literals.

**Review.** Three rounds of `gpt-5.6-sol` adversarial review in `ephemeral/reviews/202609131*-run-store-round-0*.md`; the two authority-boundary findings (model calls and turn rows taken from logs on a loaded run) are fixed with regression tests.

Also brings the two pre-existing `ephemeral/review/*/probes` fakes up to the current `HarnessAdapter` so `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` are green with no exclusions.

milestone.title: Beta
milestone.description:
Beta release: not stable, API not stable, but the software works and is useful. The bar is that Gimble is used to build Gimble.

Done when all of these are seen working on real models:

1. The API is coherent enough that a human can ask for a workflow shape and an agent, given the Godoc plus the repo's docs and skills, writes it as easily as any Go program. Loops have been written and observed enough that managing them is understood.
2. Every turn's tokens are charged to the scope it ran in, every scope and turn has wall time, and a person can see where the time and tokens went. Posted per-model token prices give a comparable cost figure as a proxy for quota use.
3. The web UI is not just alive: it looks decent and a human can use it to watch a run and send a steering message to any running agent session.
4. Proof: one real Gimble feature is built by a Gimble workflow while Tyler watches it in the web UI and steers sessions from there.

body:
The usage tree (#173) is rewriting `internal/observation/`, `web/src/lib/observation/`, and the run route, and states that it leaves the runtime, the adapters, the reducers, and the sprint workflow alone. This arc is everything in the Beta milestone that lives on the other side of that line, ordered so that each piece lands as its own small squash, so #173 rebases onto tidy commits rather than one wide one.

The arc has a spine. Beta's proof is Tyler watching a Gimble run build a Gimble feature and steering any agent from the page. Steering from the page needs the runtime to reach a live session by id, and killing an agent that has gone off the rails needs the runtime to reach a live scope or turn by id. That is the trade for `Session.Interrupt`: not a method on the pointer, but cancellation by id with a cause, built on the child contexts the library already creates. The rest of the arc is the hygiene that lets many runs and many agents coexist, and the sprint workflow and skill that make the proof run possible.

## Phases

**1. Shrink the other branch's rebase.** Land first, each touching files #173 names as unchanged.
- PR #158, Codex cache write. #173 calls it edit 1.
- #175, cancel by id with a cause, and #165 in the same PR.
- #159, infallible `Set`/`SetJSON` with the panic boundary.

**2. Operator control.**
- #107, steer reports landed or dropped.
- #113, Claude steer live.
- #176, the live run registry: `Runtime.Steer`, `KillScope`, `KillTurn` by id.
- #163, the Codex daemon descriptor limit, so a wide `Group` can be killed rather than starved.

**3. Many runs, many agents.**
- #118, one writer for `project.jsonl`.
- #111, run ids that do not collide in one second.
- #106, `just attest`, `vet`, `test`. The attest's interrupt is a ctx cancel, not `Session.Interrupt`.
- #112, `go vet` in a fresh clone.

**4. The workflow, its skill, and practice.**
- #168, the sprint workflow: a validator that cannot reshape the goal, plain local prompts, prompts visible before they run.
- #177, the workflow-writing skill and shape examples.
- #178, loop practice runs.

## Held until #173 merges

The runs index at `/`, steer and kill buttons on the page, #135 and #117 event coverage. All three edit what #173 is replacing or regenerate the skgo bindings that #173 also regenerates.

## Rules for every PR in the arc

- Nothing under `internal/observation/`, `web/src/`, or the generated skgo files. If a change forces regeneration, it waits.
- One issue per PR, squash-merged, PR body written as the commit message.
- Cheap tier for every live check. Logs under `ephemeral/attest/<issue>/`.

## Done when

Every child issue is closed, and a Go program using `web.NewRuntime` can, against a live run on the cheap tier, steer a session by id and kill a turn and a scope by id, with the log showing who did it and the Loop carrying on. That is the state from which the page half (steer and kill buttons, the runs index) is one route edit once #173 lands.

body:
The Go half of "steer or kill any agent from the page". The page half waits until the usage tree (#173) lands, because it edits the run route that #173 rewrites.

## Facts at `ad6f2f6`

- `web.Runtime` (`web/runtime.go:22`) holds a ctx, a dir, and an address. It does not know which runs are live; `Runtime.Run` calls `gimble.Run` and blocks.
- Steer needs a `*Session` (`Session.Steer`); the kill functions from the cancel-by-id issue need a `*run`. The page has neither. It has a run id, scope keys, session ids, and turn ids from the observation store.

## Change

- `Runtime` keeps `live map[runID]*liveRun` filled by `Runtime.Run` for the duration of the run. The root package exposes what the runtime needs through unexported hooks in `run.go` (a `Handle`-style value returned to `web`, or an internal package), not through new exported names on `Session`.
- Three methods on `Runtime`, by id, each returning an error for an unknown or finished target:

  ```go
  func (r *Runtime) Steer(ctx context.Context, runID, sessionID, message string) error
  func (r *Runtime) KillScope(runID, scopeKey, by, reason string) error
  func (r *Runtime) KillTurn(runID, turnID, by, reason string) error
  ```

  Steer records `Source: "person"` (the existing `steerSource` value) so the log and the page can tell an operator's steer from a supervisor's. Kill records the `Killed` lifecycle event with `By`.
- A session is found by its id (`lap.3/coder.1`) through the scope table; the session list already lives on the scope (`scope.sessions`).

## Done when

- A Go test starts a run under `web.NewRuntime` with the fake adapter, steers a session by id from another goroutine, kills a turn by id, kills a scope by id, and reads all three from the run log.
- A live check on the cheap tier where a steer from a second goroutine lands (depends on #107 to say so) and a kill ends the turn. Log under `ephemeral/attest/registry/`.
- Nothing under `web/src/` changes.

title: Cancel by id with a cause: the runtime keeps its cancel funcs, one ctx per turn, Killed replaces Session.Interrupt

body:
The trade for `Session.Interrupt` (#165). Tyler's rule stands: cancelling the ctx is the interrupt. What was missing is that the person who wants to stop an agent usually does not hold the pointer. An operator watching the run page has ids. So the runtime keeps the cancel funcs it already creates, reachable by id, and cancels with a cause so the workflow can tell a kill from an ordinary shutdown.

## Facts at `ad6f2f6`

- `scope.do` (`scope.go:78`) already creates one child ctx per scope with `context.WithCancel` and defers `end(cancel)`. `Group` does the same (`group.go:36`). Workflow code never types `cancel`; the library owns every cancel func because it creates every child ctx.
- `Generate` passes its ctx straight to `RunTurn` (`session.go:189`). There is no per-turn ctx, so one turn cannot be stopped without ending its scope.
- `run` (`run.go:34`) has no table of live scopes. The cancel funcs live on the stack of `do` and are unreachable.
- `Group` cancels every sibling on the first child error (`group.go:51`), the errgroup rule.
- `Loop` runs each task in a task scope (`loop.go:132`) and treats any error the same way.
- `web.Runtime.Run` (`web/runtime.go:187`) already wraps each run in `context.WithCancelCause`.

## Change

Stdlib only. No wrapper around `context.Context`, no new interface, no change to `HarnessAdapter`.

1. **Cause, not bare cancel.** `scope.do` and `Group` use `context.WithCancelCause`. Normal end calls `cancel(nil)` as today. A kill calls `cancel(err)` where `err` is:

   ```go
   // Killed is the cause of a ctx that an operator cancelled on purpose.
   // context.Cause(ctx) returns it in every scope and turn under the target.
   type Killed struct {
       Target string // scope key, or turn id
       By     string // who; "" when unknown
       Reason string
   }
   func (k Killed) Error() string
   ```

   Every descendant ctx reports the same cause, because a child inherits the parent's cause. Workflow code that cares checks `errors.As(context.Cause(ctx), &killed)`; code that does not care sees `ctx.Err()` as before.

2. **A table of live scopes and turns on `run`.** `scope` gains a `cancel context.CancelCauseFunc`; `run` gains `scopes map[string]*scope` (registered in `do`, removed in `end`) and `turns map[string]context.CancelCauseFunc` keyed by turn id.

3. **One ctx per turn in `Generate`.** Before `RunTurn`: `turnCtx, cancel := context.WithCancelCause(ctx)`, registered under the turn id, deregistered when `RunTurn` returns. Killing a turn ends only that turn: `Generate` returns an error wrapping the `Killed` cause, the scope keeps running, and the workflow decides whether to re-ask. This is what a "kill this agent" button on a turn row does.

4. **Two functions on `run`, unexported here, exported by the web runtime in the registry issue:** `cancelScope(key string, cause error)` and `cancelTurn(id string, cause error)`. Unknown id is an error. Both record a lifecycle event so the log says who killed what: `Killed{Target, By, Reason}` replaces the `Interrupt` lifecycle event that #165 deletes (the schema entry moves with it).

5. **Loop treats a kill as a failed task, not a broken loop.** When a task scope returns an error whose cause is `Killed`, the task is recorded failed with the reason and the planner sees it on the next lap. That is "the workflow reschedules and restarts the task".

6. **Group treats a killed child as gone, not as an abort.** A child whose error's cause is `Killed` does not cancel its siblings. `Wait` still returns the error. A bake-off survives one killed attempt.

7. **#165 in the same PR.** Delete `Session.Interrupt`, the adapter type assertion, `(*adapter).Interrupt` in `codex/` and `claude/`, and the `Interrupt` lifecycle event and schema entry. Add the missing test: after a turn is cancelled through its ctx, the same `Session` runs another turn.

## Done when

- `go test ./...` has: kill a scope from another goroutine and every session inside it is closed and the scope returns an error with the cause; kill one turn and the same session completes a second turn in the same scope; a `Group` of three with one killed child returns that child's error and the other two finish; a `Loop` with a killed task records the task failed and runs another lap.
- One live run on the cheap tier where a turn is killed by id from a second goroutine, with the run log under `ephemeral/attest/cancel-by-id/`.
- `Session.Interrupt` and the adapters' `Interrupt` methods are gone.

title: Move the Astro docs site out of the repository root
body:
## Problem

The GitHub Pages docs site is an Astro app whose files sit in the repository root. Commit 795d860 ("Restore static Astro docs for GitHub Pages", 2026-09-11) put them there:

- `astro.config.mjs`, `svelte.config.js`, `tsconfig.json`
- `package.json` (named `gimble-docs`), `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`
- `components.json` (a shadcn-svelte config pointing at `src/styles/global.css`)
- `src/` (pages, layouts, components, `src/lib/components/ui/button`, `src/styles/global.css`)
- `public/` (favicon, mascot)
- `.github/workflows/docs.yml`, which runs `pnpm install`, `pnpm run check`, and `pnpm run build` from the root and uploads `dist`

The repository root is the Go module `github.com/tylergannon/gimble`. The product web application is the SvelteKit app in `web/`, with its own `package.json`. So today the root carries a second, unrelated Node project, and:

- `components.json`, `src/`, `svelte.config.js`, and `tsconfig.json` at the root read as if they belong to the product app. They do not. While drafting the run page design brief today, this was mistaken for the app's own shadcn-svelte install.
- Two `pnpm-lock.yaml` and two `package.json` files in the tree, one of them at the root, with different pnpm versions pinned (`11.22.0` at the root, `11.25.0` in `web/`).
- `AGENTS.md` describes the layout as root package, `web/`, `cmd/`, `internal/`. The docs site is not in that description.

## Ask

Move the whole Astro site into one directory that says what it is. `site/` or `docs-site/` is fine; `docs/` is taken by `docs/definition-of-done.md`, which is repository documentation, not the website. Then:

- Update `.github/workflows/docs.yml` to run in that directory (`working-directory`, or `cd` in each step) and upload `<dir>/dist`.
- Leave the root with the Go module, `web/`, `e2e/`, `cmd/`, `internal/`, `docs/`, `ephemeral/`, `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `Justfile`, and nothing that belongs to a Node project.
- Add one line to `AGENTS.md`'s layout section naming the directory and what it is.
- Nothing in `web/` or the Go build depends on the root Node files, so `just build` and `just e2e` must be unaffected. Confirm by running both.

## Done when

- `git ls-files` at the root shows no `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `astro.config.mjs`, `svelte.config.js`, `tsconfig.json`, `components.json`, `src/`, or `public/`.
- The Pages workflow builds and deploys from the new directory on a push to main.
- `just build` and `just e2e` pass.
