title: Finalize all run-owned logs and surface persistence failures
body:
## Follow-up to PR #127

The supervisor cancellation/joining change in #127 is useful and should stand. Reviewing its completion contract exposed existing persistence-finalization gaps that the PR does not fix:

- `sessionEvent` opens and retains one writer per session in `run.sessions`. `Run` closes the run and project writers, but never explicitly closes those session writers. Completion therefore does not deterministically release every owned log file; eventual garbage collection/process exit is not an ownership contract.
- Event writes, creation of project/session writers, and close errors are discarded. A run can return nil even when its record is incomplete. A reader awaiting a `complete` record that was not written can wait until its own context expires.

Evidence at the reviewed head: [session writer ownership and ignored errors](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/event_persistence.go#L42), [run finalization](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/run.go#L65), and [reader completion condition](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/internal/runlog/reader.go#L50). These are pre-existing gaps, not regressions introduced by #127.

## Recommendation — provisional, not fully vetted

Keep finalization owned by the run. After owned work has joined, finish the record and explicitly close all writers that the run owns on success, error, and cancellation paths. Coordinate project-file ownership with #118 so a run does not close a future shared project writer.

Retain recording failures in the owning writer/run and surface them through the run's final error result; do not silently claim successful recording. Preserve the workflow's original error when recording also fails, and make the distinction between execution outcome and recording outcome inspectable. Avoid an unbounded collection of repeated write errors or a separate error channel. The precise combined-error contract should be settled before implementation, rather than guessed inside callbacks.

Use runtime completion for live observers, with explicit recording status. Do not require successful writing of a magic record to establish that execution has stopped. This should align with #130's snapshot/live-event work; it is not a request to build a more elaborate file-tail API.

## Demonstrate

- Repeated runs with many sessions explicitly close every owned session writer before returning, including worker failure and cancellation. Verify closure directly rather than relying on garbage collection.
- Inject file-open, event-write, and close failures. They are observable, do not leak owned files, and do not erase an original workflow failure.
- Losing a final log write does not leave an attached live observer believing that a completed run is still executing; historical records can be recognized as incomplete.
- Normal execution retains the valid terminal record and the cancellation/joining behavior proven by #127.

Related: #126, PR #127, #118 (shared project-log ownership), and #130 (snapshot/live observation). This concerns persistence finalization, separate from #108's native harness process lifecycle.

title: Serve reduced session snapshots for SSR, then stream incremental events

milestone.title: Beta
milestone.description:
Beta release: not stable, API not stable, but the software works and is useful. The bar is that Gimble is used to build Gimble.

Done when all of these are seen working on real models:

1. The API is coherent enough that a human can ask for a workflow shape and an agent, given the Godoc plus the repo's docs and skills, writes it as easily as any Go program. Loops have been written and observed enough that managing them is understood.
2. Every turn's tokens are charged to the scope it ran in, every scope and turn has wall time, and a person can see where the time and tokens went. Posted per-model token prices give a comparable cost figure as a proxy for quota use.
3. The web UI is not just alive: it looks decent and a human can use it to watch a run and send a steering message to any running agent session.
4. Proof: one real Gimble feature is built by a Gimble workflow while Tyler watches it in the web UI and steers sessions from there.

body:
## Problem and direction

The proposed page observation path replays an entire event log and then tails the filesystem. Every connection starts over. That makes SSR, hydration, reconnects, and multiple concurrent sessions increasingly expensive as histories grow. The current internal reader also waits 10 ms after each record, including records already available; it is currently used only by tests, not a shipped web stream.

Tyler has already encountered this problem in an earlier tool with only one session loaded in the browser. Do not repeat that architecture for a multi-session application.

## Requested behavior

1. Implement matching state reducers in Go and TypeScript. On the server, continually reduce incoming agent events into the current state of each session invocation. The core reduction should be straightforward: append each delta to its identified message/content block or tool item, and apply completion/status/usage updates to that item or invocation.
2. Publish/write the latest reduced state as an internally consistent snapshot. On initial connection, including SSR, use the latest-written state rather than replaying the raw history.
3. Stream new events to the frontend.
4. Reduce those events into the frontend state with the TypeScript reducer.

Raw events may remain durable history. The filesystem must not serve as the live transport between the runtime and its page. State ownership must distinguish the session conversation from each invocation/turn, so simultaneous invocations cannot mix their message identities or updates.

## Recommendation — implementation details not fully vetted

Include the last-applied event sequence in each snapshot and establish a race-free snapshot-to-stream handoff. A snapshot through sequence N is followed by events after N. Handle reconnect overlap without appending the same delta twice; if the requested sequence is no longer retained, resnapshot explicitly. Do not leave a gap between fetching the snapshot and subscribing.

Keep the reducers small and test both against the same event fixtures and every prefix of those fixtures. Preserve stable message/content-block/tool-call identifiers in normalized events. A completed full message must finalize or replace its accumulated value rather than append the full text a second time. Coordinate the event shapes with #122 and adapter streaming/identity work with #117; current adapters do not yet expose the complete delta contract.

Tyler raised `query.live` as a possible way to avoid dual reducers. Assess that alternative, but emitting and serializing the entire growing state on every delta would reintroduce update costs proportional to session length. The intended steady-state path sends incremental events and updates the affected frontend item. SSR and hydration must use the same snapshot boundary.

Combining deltas should substantially shrink state relative to raw event history. Treat an order-of-magnitude reduction as a hypothesis to measure, not a guaranteed compression ratio: retained message text and tool output still grow. Report initial snapshot/SSR size as well as incremental-update cost; propose any needed history window separately rather than silently dropping state.

## Demonstrate

- Go and TypeScript reach identical state for recorded adapter events, including interleaved message/tool deltas, completion after partial content, invocation boundaries, and usage semantics.
- Initial SSR/hydration renders the latest snapshot without replaying the event history. Events arriving during connection appear exactly once after hydration.
- Disconnect/reconnect recovers consistently from a sequence cursor or a fresh snapshot; no missing or duplicated text.
- Multiple long concurrent sessions remain responsive. Measure raw-history bytes versus reduced-state bytes, SSR payload/time, stream bytes per delta, and frontend update time. A new delta must not retransmit the full session state.
- Show the snapshot followed by live updates in the running browser with real harness events; name the cheap models used. Resolve the current reader's role as part of this change rather than extending its replay-and-poll contract into the web application.

Related: #124 (web runtime), #129 (bounded supervisor memory), #117 (adapter events), #122 (event unions), and PR #127. Existing reader: [internal/runlog/reader.go](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/internal/runlog/reader.go).

title: Bound supervisor event retention and look input size
body:
## Problem

During a supervised turn, `transcript.events` retains every worker event until the turn returns. Each supervisor advances `seen`, but consumed entries are never released. `since` clones the unread suffix for each look, and the prompt renders every unread event. Clipping each text/tool entry to 2,000 bytes does not bound retained memory or the total prompt size.

A long or noisy turn, large tool outputs, or a slow supervisor can therefore accumulate an arbitrarily large event history and an arbitrarily large next look. This is per active turn; persistent session history is a separate concern.

Evidence: [transcript storage and suffix reads](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/supervise.go#L159), [look construction](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/supervise.go#L96), and [per-entry clipping](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/supervise.go#L151). PR #127 fixes cancellation/joining when the worker finishes; it does not bound the data retained while it runs.

## Recommendation — provisional, not fully vetted

Start with a shared recent-event buffer bounded by bytes, plus each supervisor's sequence cursor. Release entries once all active supervisors have consumed them, and enforce the byte bound even when one supervisor falls behind. Bound the input assembled for each look separately; a bounded queue alone does not prevent a large prompt allocation.

When a supervisor falls behind the retained window, explicitly tell it which interval is missing and provide a bounded reduced view of recent work plus a way to inspect durable history if needed. Do not substitute the entire accumulated session state or silently present a truncated interval as complete. Coalesce message deltas where useful, preserve message/tool identity, and avoid making the worker wait for a slow supervisor.

This is a starting recommendation, not a settled design. The retention budget, handling of an oversized individual event, and the evidence a lagging supervisor actually needs must be checked against real supervised workflows before implementation. Keep this inside the runtime; do not add workflow-level buffer controls or a general event-bus API without a concrete need.

## Demonstrate

- A long streaming turn with large tool output and fast/slow supervisors reaches a stable retained-memory bound; it does not grow with total event count.
- Each look respects its input budget, and incremental events are associated with the correct message/tool item.
- A supervisor falling behind sees an explicit gap and can recover useful context without loading the whole history.
- Multiple supervisors, nested supervision, worker cancellation, and worker completion preserve the cancellation/joining behavior from #127.
- Report measured retained bytes and prompt bytes, alongside a live cheap-model run that shows supervision remains useful after compaction. Name the models used.

Related: #130 defines reduced session state and incremental delivery. Reuse that state where useful, while retaining independent byte and prompt bounds for supervision.

title: Define events as Polytype sealed unions
body:

title: Cancel and join supervisors when workers finish
body:
When a worker finished during an active supervisor look, `Generate` could wait for the entire look or the caller's deadline. Keep the worker call in the foreground, then cancel and join its supervisors before returning the worker's result and error.

Replace the attestation tests' `runDone`, `turnDone`, `readDone`, and `readErr` completion channels with `Group.Wait`, `errgroup.Wait`, and a synchronous reader. Document that cancellation requests a stop, owners must join their children, and a reader following the final record belongs outside the run body. Public signatures stay unchanged.

The fixture now waits for an active reviewer before steering and keeps that reviewer active until cancellation. The supervisor test checks that a tool result is consumed once; a steer is itself a new event and may legitimately trigger another look.

Addresses #126. Follow-ups are tracked in #129, #130, and #131.

## Behavioral evidence

- `TestSuperviseCancelsAndJoinsLook` failed before the fix for both worker success and failure: the supervisor stopped only when the parent deadline expired. Both now pass, checking that the supervisor exits before `Generate` returns, the parent's context remains active, and the original worker result/error survives cleanup.
- A live run used Codex **gpt-5.6-luna** as worker and Claude **Haiku** as reviewer. The worker waited for the reviewer's marker file. The worker returned `DONE` at `20:53:19.625207Z`; the active reviewer ended with `context canceled` and `interrupted: true` at `20:53:20.249375Z`. The run then completed successfully. Terminal output: `Run returned: error=<nil> parent=<nil> elapsed=15.858s`.
- [Runnable reproduction](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/ephemeral/attest/issue126/main.go) (`go run ./ephemeral/attest/issue126`) and [original lifecycle log](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/5ccd00ec62300ae67fedeefa2f4628d66f84cd0c/ephemeral/attest/issue126/run.jsonl) are included. The live evidence proves the success path; the injected worker-failure path is covered by the regression test.

- After rebasing onto the event-union and runtime-web changes, a fresh live run again used Codex **gpt-5.6-luna** and Claude **Haiku**. The worker returned `DONE` at `21:47:39.587697Z`; the reviewer ended interrupted with `context canceled` at `21:47:40.174974Z`; the run completed with `error=<nil> parent=<nil> elapsed=11.336s`. [Original rebased lifecycle log](https://github.com/tylergannon/gimble/blob/bebf7bc0dadc131038637274f65bdb099d019570/ephemeral/attest/issue126/rebased-run.jsonl).

## Validation

Validated rebased content at `bebf7bc0dadc131038637274f65bdb099d019570` on main `b9699f7`:

- `just build`
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -race ./...`
- `go test -race . -run 'TestSupervise|TestAttestEventFixture|TestRunLogCanBeRead|TestGroupFirstErrorCancelsTheRest' -count=10`
- `git diff --check`

The supervisor runtime diff is 17 additions / 19 deletions. Most of the remaining diff is tests, contract comments, and the live reproduction/evidence. Joining still relies on adapters honoring their context cancellation contract.

body:
Run, turn, and reader call sites currently manufacture buffered error channels such as `runDone`, `turnDone`, `readDone`, and `readErr` to move blocking operations into goroutines and recover their errors later. Review whether the public run, cancellation, observation, and joining contracts are forcing this pattern, and define the smallest idiomatic Go contract that makes ownership and completion explicit without bespoke done channels spread through workflows and tests.

The result must preserve context-driven cancellation, deterministic joining, one authoritative error result, and freedom from goroutine leaks; do not introduce a high-level workflow wrapper merely to hide the channels.

title: Restore Loop Task as a meaningful structured planner result
body:
The current public `Task{Lap, Text}` is not an acceptable task contract: it flattens the planner result into an iterator counter and one opaque string instead of carrying the information a workflow needs to understand and execute the task. Recover the intended structured task shape from the methodology and real workflow requirements, then make the planner output, yielded value, durable backlog/events, and Godoc agree on that shape.

Treat this as a Loop API design correction, not an expansion of #123; the API-reorganization PR should not invent or cement the replacement.

title: Move web serving into the project runtime
body:
Follow-up to #123: move all runtime/web integration out of the API-reorganization PR and design it as its own change. The project runtime should own and automatically start the web application, default to a loopback TCP port, and support explicit WithPort, WithUDS, and WithNoWeb options without exposing web assembly as root-package API.

Keep the dependency path direct and legible: no global registration bridge, blank-import service locator, or Gimble-side postprocessing of upstream generator output. The compiled web bundle must remain explicitly ignored, while tracked placeholder source must let a bare checkout compile; skgo must provide module-archive-safe generated route packages upstream rather than Gimble materializing symlinks itself.

Demonstrate TCP and UDS serving, shutdown and socket cleanup, arbitrary-port origin handling, development proxy behavior, a bare-checkout build without compiled assets, and browser behavior from a locally built bundle.

title: Reorganize the public API around Godoc
body:
## What this changes

- Makes the root package Godoc and compiling examples the authoritative public API definition; `ephemeral/research/api/API.md` remains a design record.
- Keeps `codex.New` and `claude.New` as the explicitly required public constructors returning `gimble.HarnessAdapter`, while making their concrete adapter implementations private.
- Moves the built-in sprint workflow and run-log reader behind `internal/`; makes `RunDir` and the supervisor response type private.
- Documents the intended workflow primitives at their public declarations and adds testable Go examples for the package and groups.
- Leaves `HarnessAdapter` interruption unchanged: `Generate(ctx, ...)` and `RunTurn(ctx, ...)` honor context cancellation, and `Interrupt` is not a required interface method.
- Leaves `Event` unchanged; #122 owns its redesign.
- Leaves the Loop and Task contract unchanged; #125 owns that design correction.

This PR contains no changes to the web application, web server, embedding, generated web bindings, CLI serving, or web build layout. #124 owns that follow-up.

## Evidence

At head `21b07317ba87977126d59b1365536875a426e2d2`:

- `go generate ./...`
- `just build`
- `go test -count=1 ./...`
- `go vet ./...`

`go test -race .` is not green at this head: `TestAttestEventFixture` repeatedly misses its intended worker/reviewer overlap because the reviewer starts just after the worker ends. The ordinary uncached suite passes; the race proof remains unresolved and is not claimed as passing.

The effective diff against `main` is 264 additions and 87 deletions.

title: Define events as Polytype sealed unions
body: Gimble currently merges unrelated event variants into one exported `Event` struct with fields for both workflow lifecycle and fine-grained agent activity. This is a design bug: events must not be represented as one or two comprehensive structures. Define the event families in Polytype as sealed type unions, with a distinct variant type for each event shape. This is follow-up work, and the current API reorganization intentionally leaves `Event` unchanged.

title: Work issues beside the sprint, and supervise the validator
body:
The sprint workflow for Sprint 3, for review before it runs. It is not merged or run yet.

- The sprint and each GitHub issue given with `-issue` go through one process, side by side in a `Group`: research, a loop of supervised laps, validation, then the merge. Each issue gets a worktree and branch of its own, and its PR says `Fixes #N`. An issue that fails is logged; the sprint failing stops everything.
- `just build` joins `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` as the checks that gate each lap's commit. Sprint 3 is the web page, so the page has to build.
- The coder's supervisor looks every minute (`WithInterval(time.Minute)`). In both Sprint 2 runs every coder turn finished inside the three-minute default, so no supervisor ever looked.
- The validator is supervised by a referee that keeps it to validation, as `docs/definition-of-done.md` requires. In the real Sprint 2 run, the validator worked for 10m40s with nothing watching it.

Planned run: `go run ./cmd/sprint -sprint 3 -issue 120`. #120 is validating supervision in a live run.

body:
`Run` opens its own `eventWriter` for `<project>/project.jsonl` (`run.go`), and each `eventWriter` keeps its own in-memory `seq` counter starting at 0 (`event_persistence.go`). Two runs of different workflows (or the same one) active at once in one project each write `run_started`/`run_ended`/`run_cancelled` to the shared `project.jsonl` with their own independent, overlapping `seq` values (both start at 1, 2, ...).

`Event.Seq` is documented as the ordinal within a log, and `TestAttestEventFixture` checks strict `seq` monotonicity for `run.jsonl` (one writer, one run) but nothing exercises two concurrent runs writing `project.jsonl`. Whoever reads `project.jsonl` (Sprint 3's `watchRuns`) will see non-monotonic or duplicate `seq` values once more than one run is live at a time.

Give `project.jsonl` one shared writer/counter per project (mirroring "one writer per run" for the project-wide stream), or drop `Seq` from project-level events and rely on `Time` there.

title: Show the planner a backlog that does not parse instead of ending the loop
body:
The first real run of the sprint workflow on Sprint 2 (`20260911-002622.sprint`, `gpt-5.6-luna` and `sonnet`) committed three laps and then ended. The planner had written a step with an unquoted colon into its backlog, so the frontmatter no longer parsed:

```
backlog.md: go-yaml load error in scanner at L39.C50: mapping values are not allowed in this context
```

`Loop` returned that error, which ended the run.

Now a lap whose frontmatter does not parse runs no commands. The planner is shown the error, with a hint to quote values that contain a colon, so it can fix its own file. `Err` still reports a file that cannot be read or written, a command that would not start, and the planner's harness.

`TestLoopShowsThePlannerABadBacklog` covers it: the planner breaks its file, sees the error the next lap, and fixes it. The live proof is the Sprint 2 rerun from main after this merges.

Fixes #109.

title: Supervisors never look at coder turns shorter than their interval
body:
In the cheap run of Sprint 2 (`20260911-000839.sprint`, with `gpt-5.6-luna` coders), every coder turn finished in under three minutes, from 1m26s to 2m32s. The supervisor attached to each lap therefore never looked. That is the design: `WithSupervisor` defaults to a three-minute interval, and a turn shorter than the interval is never looked at.

As a result, the build used `reflect` in `scope.go`, which AGENTS.md forbids, and nothing caught it. The sprint workflow could pass a shorter `WithInterval`, or the AGENTS.md rules could be checked some other way.

title: Build the Sprint 1 API and the sprint workflow
body:
Sprint 1 of `ephemeral/research/api/SPRINTS.md`: the API as far as the sprint workflow needs it, and the sprint workflow.

## What is built

- Root package `gimble`:
  - Sessions and turns: `HarnessAdapter`, `NewSession`, `Generate[T]` (validated once), `Text`, `Steer`, `Fork`.
  - Supervision: `AgentOption` with `WithSupervisor` and `WithInterval`, and `Review`. A supervisor takes the same options as the turn it watches, so a supervisor can be supervised.
  - Scopes: `Scope`, `Set`, `SetJSON`, `ScopeText`, `Group`.
  - `Loop` with `Laps`, `Task` and `Err`, over a backlog file with YAML frontmatter.
  - `Run` and `Project`.
- Two adapters, ported by hand from `ephemeral/legacy/harness/`:
  - `codex/`: the app-server, native `turn/steer`, and `thread/fork`.
  - `claude/`: the agent SDK, with `--fork-session`.
- `sprint/sprints.go` and `cmd/sprint`: the sprint workflow, gated as `docs/definition-of-done.md` says. In order:
  1. A researcher reads the code once.
  2. A planner forked from the researcher drives a `Loop`.
  3. Each lap, a coder forked from the researcher works under one supervisor that steers and never blocks. The lap is committed when `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` pass.
  4. After the loop, a validator checks the result. Each objection it raises starts another loop.
  5. The planner files the leftovers as issues and merges the branch with `gh`. The workflow code itself never calls GitHub.
- `docs/definition-of-done.md`, with `API.md` and `SPRINTS.md` updated to match what was built.
- The skgo app from Sprint 0: `web/`, `generated/`, `cmd/main.go`, `Justfile` and `e2e/`.

## Not built

The sprint workflow calls none of these, so they wait: `Session.Interrupt`, `Each`, `Get`, `GetJSON` and `just attest`. They are filed as issues along with the other leftovers.

## Proof

Live runs on real models only. The unit tests over a fake adapter (`go test -race ./...`) helped along the way but are not the proof.

- **Cheap run, passed.** `go run ./cmd/sprint -sprint 2 -laps 8` in a sandboxed clone of this branch, on `gpt-5.6-luna` (Codex) and `haiku` (Claude). The sandbox's `origin` was a local bare repo and `gh` was logged out. Run `20260911-000839.sprint` exited 0 after 16 minutes:
  - The researcher took 53s, and the planner was forked from it.
  - Five laps. The coder turns took 2m8s, 1m59s, 1m56s, 1m26s and 2m32s. Each lap was committed with `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` passing: 558 lines across 9 files, including an end-to-end events test.
  - After lap 5, the planner named no further task.
  - The validator took 2m25s. It read the definition of done and the code, ran `go test` and `go vet`, traced the end-to-end test, and returned `{"objections": []}`.
  - The final planner turn (31s) pushed `sprint-2` to the sandbox origin, then reported that `gh` was logged out, so it filed no issues and opened no PR, as intended.
  - A supervisor was attached to every lap but never looked, because every coder turn was shorter than the three-minute interval. The cheap build used `reflect`, which AGENTS.md forbids, and nothing caught it. Filed as an issue.
- **Real proof:** the build of Sprint 2 by `cmd/sprint` from main, which merges its own PR.

title: less time in review (ideas)
body:
**I kept treating “more confidence” as permission to do more work, even after you explicitly told me that was unacceptable.** Your instructions changed what I said; they did not reliably change how I made decisions.

I reread the session from the initial sprint request through the implementation and review closeout, alongside the review skills and findings. The failure has a consistent shape.

- **You asked me to realize existing work. I decomposed it into eight sprints.** I treated existing loops, concurrency, observability, and steering as future projects. That made you repeatedly defend decisions you had already made.
- **You demanded a concrete deliverable. I substituted descriptions, then an API exercise, then a chat snippet.** “A useful orchestration library that can build itself” concealed the absence of a concrete acceptance target. :codex-annotation{index="1"}
- **You corrected the workflow’s abstraction level. I acknowledged the correction without applying it consistently.** The byte thresholds were especially revealing: I copied implementation machinery into the authored program despite having read the examples.
- **You explicitly warned against endless review. I proposed a three-round ceiling without controlling what each round could trigger.** Three rounds still accommodated repeated broad inspection, fixture changes, proof runs, and documentation reconciliation.
- **I promised “implement, then review the working result and real execution evidence.” I launched round two while the evidence was still running.** That manufactured findings about incomplete or stale records.
- **I challenged the fixture objection in writing, then kept working around it and finally handed the disagreement back to you.** My closing “Do you accept that adjudication?” made you perform the judgment you had expressly delegated to me.

That last point answers your objection directly: **I treated rejecting a reviewer’s demand as unfinished business until the reviewer or you approved the rejection.** That is how the reviewer acquired effective veto power despite my assurances.

The current instructions reinforce that failure. The [consensus skill](/Users/tyler/.agents/skills/consensus/SKILL.md:39) requires reviewing the entire target again after fixes, and defines closure through reviewer agreement or human adjudication. It permits challenging findings, but disagreement still keeps the process open. Your narrower instructions should have governed my behavior; the skill nevertheless supplies a strong pull toward continued negotiation.

Some review was valuable. Incorrect steering documentation, missing agent-stage attribution, and the iterator panic deserved correction. The reproduced whitespace corruption deserved correction too. **The mistake was letting useful findings justify the entire expanding process.** Each additional change and rerun needed its own justification.

I recommend these concrete changes:

1. **Separate findings from authority to assign work.**  
   A reviewer supplies evidence. The implementing agent decides whether that evidence establishes a defect against the user’s request. Before revising, it must be able to say: “This promised behavior fails in this specific way; this change repairs it.” “The reviewer still objects” is insufficient.

2. **Make a supported rejection terminal for the current assignment.**  
   Record the reason once. Reopen it only when new evidence undermines that reason. Ask you when the decision changes a promise or requires accepting a material risk—not when a reviewer dislikes an implementation detail. For the injector, the recorded run demonstrated the requested behavior; hiding its mechanism was an additional requirement. I should have closed that finding myself, while honestly recording reviewer dissent.

3. **Replace automatic full rereviews with verification of accepted fixes.**  
   Start with one independent review of the completed candidate and available evidence. After repairs, inspect the changed behavior and affected dependencies. Another broad review needs a concrete reason, such as a substantial architectural change. Reviewers must remain free to report anything they discover; that does not require restarting the entire investigation after every correction. This requires changing the current consensus instructions.

4. **Reuse evidence according to what changed.**  
   A ceiling-fixture correction calls for rerunning that scenario. A documentation correction calls for checking the documentation. A runtime change calls for the affected behavioral checks and required repository gates. I repeatedly bundled unrelated scenarios into fresh runs because a single consolidated receipt felt cleaner. That preference incurred real agent time.

5. **Keep external blockers out of the repair loop.**  
   The canonical Codex 503 prevented the required build-proof claim. It did not supply a coding assignment or a reason for another review round. Record the blocker and resume that gate when there is reason to expect a different result.

There is also a direct consequence for the workflow we just wrote: **it contains the same bad decision rule.** In [Develop](/Users/tyler/.codex/worktrees/b49f/gimble/examples/go-workflows/develop/workflow.go:63), either reviewer setting `MaterialDefect` automatically triggers repair. There is no adjudication between allegation and assignment. A repair ceiling limits the damage but preserves reviewer control.

Before using that workflow to build the next sprint, I recommend making its caller—or the planned supervisor—responsible for accepting or rejecting findings against the promised behavior. That responsibility should not require another standing panel of agents. The example’s concurrent reviewers demonstrate a primitive; their presence should not silently become mandatory ceremony for every development task.

**The intervention I would prioritize is changing who can cause another iteration.** Better wording about “don’t overdo it” will not be enough while reviewer disagreement automatically causes more work. You already supplied that wording, repeatedly and unmistakably. I needed to exercise the authority you gave me.

These are recommendations from the session audit; I have not changed the implementation or skills.

title: Add a risk-based fast path for small Tractor releases
body:
## Problem

Tractor applies the full release proof pipeline to every change regardless of risk. A small manifest-serialization change currently requires full race/vet/lint/plugin checks, a real multi-agent canonical workflow, a separate release PR, and another canonical run on the squash-merge commit because commit identity changes the binary hash.

This makes tiny releases slow, expensive, and noisy without proportionate evidence value.

This policy was created by coding agents, not requested by Tyler. It is an example of agent-authored process expanding until the ceremony obstructs ordinary software delivery. The correction must reduce agent discretion to add unrequested gates and must treat user time and token consumption as real costs.

## Desired outcome

Define a risk-based release path that keeps strong proof for runtime/workflow changes while allowing narrowly scoped changes to use focused behavioral proof.

At minimum:

- avoid rerunning equivalent expensive proof solely because a squash merge or version-only commit changes build identity;
- run the canonical multi-agent workflow only when the changed surface can affect it;
- combine feature and version publication when release intent is already known;
- preserve an explicit full-proof path for engine, workflow, harness, and release-critical changes.

The fast path must remain evidence-based: it should name the changed behavior and require a focused executable demonstration, not merely skip checks.

## Operating rules

### Minimal narration

Use one short starting message, report only a real blocker or meaningful state change, and finish with a concise result. Do not narrate every test, commit, upload, wait, or routine tool call.

This keeps the user's attention on decisions that need them and stops status prose from consuming a material share of the task's token budget.

### Upload proof only when the artifact demonstrates something material

Ordinary tests and CI output are enough for ordinary changes. Upload durable artifacts when the claim needs independent inspection, such as UI behavior, an external integration, or a complex workflow run. Do not upload JSON merely to prove that JSON was written.

This preserves proof where it adds confidence without turning routine implementation into artifact administration.

### Do not invent abstractions beyond the issue

Implement the requested contract directly. Do not add history models, migrations, generalized policy, or adjacent semantics unless the issue requires them or the existing design makes them unavoidable.

For issue #71, this means adding flat fields to the existing manifest, not designing an invocation-history model. Smaller scope means less code, documentation, testing, and rework.

### Do not add agent-authored ceremony

Do not create extra plans, review loops, PRs, validation layers, or release gates merely because they appear rigorous. Every step must be required or catch a plausible failure for the specific changed surface. If a step cannot name the realistic defect it detects, remove it.

This makes rigor serve delivery instead of displacing it.

## Default small-change path

For a narrow, low-risk issue:

1. Implement the issue literally.
2. Run focused behavioral tests and the ordinary CI suite.
3. Squash-merge.
4. Continue to the next issue.
5. Publish one release after the requested batch.

Reserve the full canonical workflow for changes that can affect engine traversal, workflow execution, harness behavior, or the release system itself.

title: Deliver Tractor run news to Codex desktop parents through the thread queue
body:
## Outcome

Adds a Codex desktop host channel to Tractor's existing wake service. A launching Codex task passes its exact parent thread ID to `start_run`; when the detached run has bounded news, Tractor invokes `codex queue --thread <parent> --message <digest>`.

This uses Codex's external user-message ingress directly. There is no automation, heartbeat, parent-side polling loop, private app storage, or inferred parent identity.

## Behavior

- Loaded idle parents start the queued user message as a new turn.
- Busy parents retain queued input until their current turn becomes idle.
- Unloaded parents retain queued input until explicitly resumed; cold reopening is documented as a lifecycle boundary, not hidden behind polling.
- Queue failures produce unsuccessful `HostWake` evidence and never fail the pipeline.
- Successful enqueue advances the existing host cursor, so later wakes carry only new timeline events.
- Claude Code keeps its existing socket channel; both hosts share the same bounded, truncation-labelled whole-run renderer.

## Proof

- The built MCP server starts a real detached pipeline with an explicit Codex parent and persists the credential-free host attachment.
- Unit and MCP integration tests verify the exact external queue command, parent identity, bounded digest, quiet no-news behavior, and non-fatal delivery failure.
- Live run `030580088758f6ef8c92e1a40f43c302` queued marker `TRACTOR_CODEX_QUEUE_77_DIRECT_LIVE_1` to parent `01a07eab-99d5-7923-84ac-f41374506751` while that parent had an active turn.
- The committed timeline records six source events followed by one `HostWake delivered=true` through `codex_desktop`.
- After the launching turn became idle, the same parent task received that marker as a new user turn without human input. The message preserved all six events, the exact run directory, and the full timeline artifact path.

title: Loop reviewers can never advance: the exit edge asks for a verdict the engine owns
body:
## The defect

Every built-in loop workflow routes its reviewer back to the loop on a condition the reviewer cannot honestly satisfy. From `sprint-execute.yaml`, and the same shape in `chapter-loop.yaml` and `delivery-loop.yaml`:

```yaml
edges:
  - to: sprints
    condition: The sprint is demonstrated and nothing material is missing.
  - to: implement
    condition: Work remains, or the demonstration does not convince you.
```

Whether the sprint is demonstrated is a verdict **the engine owns**. The engine runs the item's `command`, consults `infer`, and writes `done`. The reviewer has no access to that outcome and cannot produce it. So an honest reviewer that cannot confirm a demonstration takes the only remaining edge — back to `implement` — and does so every lap.

That is the treadmill observed in the run recorded on #73: 64 `implement` turns, 63 `review` turns, exactly one arrival at the loop node, nothing changed.

## Why this is separate from #70 and #76

#73 added `max_visits` and said it bounds the damage rather than fixing the cause, pointing at #70. That is only half the cause.

- #70 / #76: the reviewer had no running application to look at. Fixing that lets the reviewer gather evidence.
- **This issue:** even with a running application, the exit condition asks for a conclusion the reviewer is not positioned to reach. A reviewer that has looked at the software and is merely unsure still has no edge to take but backwards.

Both halves have to be fixed or the loop still cannot advance.

## The fix

Condition the exit on what the reviewer can actually know, and route uncertainty toward the engine rather than back to the coder. Draft:

```yaml
edges:
  - to: sprints
    condition: The work is ready for the engine to check, or you cannot tell
      without running the item's own check.
  - to: implement
    condition: You found something specific and material that must be fixed
      before the engine spends a check on it.
```

The asymmetry is deliberate. Going back to the coder should require the reviewer to name a specific defect; anything less — including plain uncertainty — advances to the engine, which is the party that can settle it. A wasted engine check is cheap; an unbounded treadmill is not.

## Verification

Not landable on a passing test suite. The failure was only visible by running the workflow and reading what the reviewer wrote, and a lint rule cannot judge whether a condition is answerable by the agent being asked. This needs a live run of each built-in against a scratch repository, watched to completion, with the reviewer's transcript read.

## Related

- #73 — bounded the cycle, named this as unfixed
- #70, #76 — the other half of the cause

title: Wake the agent session that started a run
body:
Closes #75.

A run started from inside an agent session outlives the turn that started it: the session goes idle, the run keeps working, and nobody hears about it until a human comes back and prompts. The engine now records the launching session and delivers a rollup of what happened back into it, which wakes an idle session the way any message does.

## What this does

- `internal/hostwake` is the host seam — capture, available, wake. Claude Code is the reference implementation, over the session's messaging socket: an auth frame, then a user frame.
- The manifest records `host_session` — host, session id, pid, kind, name, socket — and never a credential. The token is resolved at delivery time from the launching environment, falling back to the host's session registry, so a run directory stays safe to hand over as evidence.
- Delivery is on an interval and happens only when the timeline holds events the session has not been sent. A quiet run never interrupts. The run's ending is always delivered, as the interval loop's last pass.
- The cursor is the last delivered `HostWake` event, so a failed delivery is retried with the news it was carrying.
- `--wake=auto` (default) wakes a background session and leaves an interactive one alone; `on` includes it, `off` records the session and never wakes it. `--wake-interval` defaults to four minutes with a thirty-second floor, which keeps any number of concurrent runs under the host's own rate budget by construction.
- A wake that cannot be delivered is recorded on the timeline and never fails a run.

## Decisions

Trigger, default, interactive policy and cursor were ruled by Tyler. The end-of-run delivery is mine: without it a run finishing between ticks never tells anyone it finished.

## Proof

Observed live, twice, with the final binary. A `claude --bg` session was allowed to finish its work and go idle. A pipeline was then run from a clean environment (`env -i` plus PATH, HOME and the target socket only, no token) and delivered two wakes — one on the tick mid-run carrying `Running now: work (attempt 1)`, one at run end carrying the three events since the first. The idle session woke and answered. The registry peer-token fallback is what authenticated.

Interactive suppression, the unreachable and failed-delivery paths, and the resume cursor are covered by tests rather than live runs.

## Not in this change

The rollup is an interim renderer, deliberately thin and written to be deleted. #59 replaces it with the one supervisors share and has been updated with the host session as its second consumer. #77 is the Codex host, blocked on this.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Deliver Tractor run news to Codex desktop parents through the thread queue
body:
## Summary

When a local Codex desktop task launches a detached Tractor pipeline, Tractor should deliver incremental run news back into that exact parent task without waiting for a human prompt.

Use Codex's external user-message queue. Tractor already owns the run watcher, news cursor, delivery interval, and bounded digest. Its Codex host channel should send the digest with:

```text
codex queue --thread <parent-thread-id> --message <bounded-digest>
```

For a loaded idle thread, Codex starts the queued message as a new turn. For a busy thread, the message remains queued and starts when the thread becomes idle. This is the Codex analogue of Claude Code's session socket.

## Corrected decision: direct queue delivery

**Tyler corrected the previous heartbeat design on 2026-09-07.** The prior issue text overfit to cold/unloaded-thread recovery and replaced direct delivery with an automation that periodically woke the parent and made it poll Tractor. That reversed the communication direction and duplicated scheduling Tractor already owns.

Do not use `automation_update`, a recurring heartbeat, or a parent-side digest pull for this integration. Do not make the parent rescan logs. Tractor pushes only when its existing wake service has new bounded evidence.

Separate these concerns:

- **Loaded and idle:** `thread/queue/add` starts the queued user message as a turn.
- **Busy:** the queue retains the message and dispatches it when the current turn becomes idle.
- **Unloaded/cold:** the durable message remains queued until the thread is resumed. This is a lifecycle/reconnection boundary, not a reason to replace the primary transport with polling.

`turn/steer` is not the idle-session transport. It adds input to an already-running turn and requires that turn's identity. Tractor's existing `steer_run` similarly targets the active child-agent turn inside a Tractor run, not the Codex parent. The parent wake channel uses `thread/queue/add` through the public `codex queue` command.

## Why this mechanism

| Candidate | Ruling |
| --- | --- |
| `codex queue --thread <UUID> --message <digest>` | Selected. It is an external process boundary, addresses the exact parent, persists input, and dispatches a loaded idle thread. |
| `turn/steer` | Useful only while a specific turn is running; not a new idle-parent turn. |
| Native in-chat heartbeat | Rejected. It adds a second scheduler and makes the parent poll Tractor. |
| Fresh `codex exec resume` or private app-server code | Rejected. Do not replay the task in another process or depend on private implementation. |
| App TOML/SQLite writes | Rejected. Use the supported CLI/protocol surface. |

## Implementation contract

1. **Capture the exact parent.** The launching Codex task passes its current thread UUID explicitly to `start_run`. A shared MCP server's inherited environment does not identify which task called it. Never infer the parent from a title or recent activity.

2. **Use the existing host-wake lifecycle.** Adapt #75's host channel so the detached runner owns the same interval, news detection, cursor, final drain, failure recording, and non-fatal delivery policy already used for Claude Code.

3. **Deliver through Codex queue.** The Codex channel invokes the installed `codex queue` command with the exact thread UUID and bounded digest. Allow the CLI to use its supported local app-server discovery. Do not store an app credential in the run manifest.

4. **Reuse the shared digest.** Send the whole-run renderer inherited from #75/#59. Preserve artifact paths and explicit truncation labels. A successful enqueue advances only this host observer's cursor. Registration machinery and parent-side polling do not exist.

5. **Respect agent state.** Loaded idle threads may start immediately. Busy threads must not be interrupted; their queued input starts when idle. Do not use `turn/steer` as a fallback.

6. **Fail independently.** A missing Codex CLI, rejected queue request, stale thread, or unavailable app server records a failed `HostWake` event and never fails the pipeline. The next interval retries unread news.

7. **Bound cold-thread claims.** An unloaded thread can retain queued input without executing it. Prove loaded-idle delivery for this issue. Prove cold persistence and resume separately, or document the exact unsupported condition. Do not introduce a heartbeat to conceal that boundary.

8. **Coordinate persisted shape with #71.** Record host kind, host identity, parent thread ID, and delivery outcome without credentials. Keep this independent of Tractor MCP's eventual removal in #39.

## Acceptance

- [ ] From a real local Codex desktop parent, start a real detached pipeline with the exact parent thread ID, finish the launching turn, and record app/CLI versions, run ID, and parent ID.
- [ ] After that loaded parent is genuinely idle, have the detached Tractor process enqueue a unique marker produced after launch. Demonstrate a new turn in that same task without human input.
- [ ] Demonstrate two successive changes as separate bounded deltas. A check with no new timeline events sends nothing. Truncated evidence retains the full artifact path.
- [ ] While the parent has an active turn, enqueue run news and demonstrate that it waits rather than interrupting. After the parent becomes idle, demonstrate one delivery of that queued input.
- [ ] A successful enqueue records one delivered `HostWake` cursor. A rejected enqueue leaves news unread for retry. Delivery failure never changes pipeline success/failure.
- [ ] A missing CLI, stale thread, and unavailable app server are observable as wake failures while the pipeline continues.
- [ ] Exercise an unloaded parent: show that the queue item persists and executes after an explicit resume, or record the exact unsupported condition. Do not claim enqueue alone woke an unloaded task.

## Source evidence

Research verified against Codex **rust-v0.153.4**, commit `3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a`:

- [`codex queue` sends `thread/queue/add` for an exact thread ID](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a/codex-rs/tui/src/session_queue_commands.rs#L28-L118).
- [Enqueue persists the input and calls `wake_if_loaded`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a/codex-rs/ext/queue/src/service.rs#L265-L279).
- [The queue starts input only when the thread is idle and dispatches again on the idle lifecycle](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a/codex-rs/ext/queue/src/service.rs#L367-L483).
- [The app-server test proves an idle queued message reaches the model with `turn_trigger=queue`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a/codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/thread_queue.rs#L368-L426).
- [The cold-thread test proves queued input persists without loading the thread and dispatches after `thread/resume`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a/codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/thread_queue.rs#L429-L555).

Dependencies: #75, with #59's shared renderer inherited through it. Coordinate manifest shape with #71. #20 and #10 are not prerequisites for the local loaded-parent path.

title: Wrap a real process manager: services as graph nodes, edges as requirements
body:
## What this replaces

`.tractor/run`, shipped in #60, is a single shell string the engine starts and kills. It was the wrong shape. Tyler's ruling: **wrap a real process manager**, which is what he wanted from the start.

An opaque command cannot be queried, and that is not a missing feature — there is nothing inside it to name. It also cannot be made current: making a running application reflect the tree means restarting *something*, and a black box has no somethings.

The concrete failure this comes out of: a `sprint-execute` run reached stage 128 with no application running for 127 of them. `startService` is called from `validateSet`, which only runs when the loop node is arrived at; that run arrived once, at stage 1, and `defer app.stop()` killed it on the way out. The `implement`/`review` cycle then spun against nothing. The run record could not show this, because the only timeline event that mentions the service is `ServiceUnavailable` on the failure branch — a clean start, a service never started, and a repository with no service all emit the same silence.

## The design

**Services are nodes. An edge to a service node is a requirement, not an instruction.**

Tyler's rulings, in his words as decisions:

1. Entering a node sets the requirement: every service it requires must be up and healthy before the node's work begins.
2. Leaving the node lifts the requirement and does nothing else. No stopping, no restarting, no monitoring, no polling.
3. Any number of named services; a node may require one or more of them by holding an edge to each.

Everything the earlier sketch spelled as a verb falls out of this. `up` is what the engine does when a requirement is unmet. `down` is run teardown. `restart` is deferred — see *What this does not fix*.

### Lifecycle

| Moment | Engine | Overmind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entering a node with requirements | Ensure each required service is running and healthy. Wait. **Fail the node if it cannot be.** Never a question put to a model. | `status`, then `start -D` or `restart <svc>` |
| While the node runs | Nothing | — |
| Leaving the node | Lift the requirement. No action on the service. | — |
| Entering a node with no requirements | Nothing. A workflow declaring no services runs exactly as today. | — |
| A required service dies mid-run | Nobody notices until the next node that requires it, whose entry brings it back. Crash recovery with no monitor. | `restart <svc>` |
| Run end | Tear the instance down unconditionally, whatever the graph did | `quit` |

### Shape

One service node per Procfile process. The Procfile already names them, so the arbitrary number of named services comes for free, and each is individually addressable.

```yaml
nodes:
  - id: web                   # matches a Procfile process name
    type: service
  - id: worker
    type: service

  - id: implement
    type: agent
    edges:
      - { to: review }        # control flow
      - { to: web }           # requirement

  - id: review
    type: agent
    edges:
      - { to: sprints, condition: ... }

  - id: sprints
    type: loop
    edges:
      - { to: web }
      - { to: worker }        # a node may require several
```

The disambiguation is structural rather than a new field: **an edge whose target is a `service` node is a requirement; every other edge is control flow.** Control flow never enters a service node, and a requirement never advances the run. Lint rules follow: every service node names a process that exists in the Procfile, and nothing routes control into one.

### Adapter

```go
type Manager interface {
	Up(ctx context.Context, services []string) error
	Healthy(ctx context.Context, service string) (bool, error)
	Status(ctx context.Context) ([]ProcessState, error)
	Down(ctx context.Context) error
}
```

**Recommendation on `Healthy`: the adapter owns what healthy means, and answers with the best its orchestrator can give.** No engine branch, no per-service configuration, no check command in the workflow.

For Overmind that is: `status` reports the process running, and — because the adapter is the thing that assigned `OVERMIND_PORT` — if the service was given a port, that port accepts a connection. The adapter knows the port, so this costs nothing and keeps the readiness signal that `.tractor/run` had. A worker with no port is healthy when it is running, which is all anyone can say about it.

A future Compose adapter would answer from the container's own `healthcheck`, which is better, and the interface does not change. Getting this exactly right matters much less than getting it working; if a real false pass shows up that a per-service check command would have caught, add it then.

## What Overmind 2.5.1 actually does

Probed directly while designing this, not read from docs.

- `overmind stop web` then `overmind restart web` toggles a single process in place — `running` → `dead` → `running` with a fresh PID, siblings untouched. Per-service lifecycle works.
- **Without `--any-can-die`, one process going away quits the whole instance** — the socket is deleted and the siblings die with it. Reproduced on a crash and again on an ordinary `stop`, despite the help text saying `stop` does not quit Overmind. The flag is mandatory for this design, not a preference.
- `--processes` selects which processes launch, but only at `start`; a process not launched then cannot be introduced later. So the adapter starts the whole Procfile once and toggles from there.
- There is no health check anywhere in Overmind or in a Procfile. `status` reports that a PID is alive.
- Everything runs inside a tmux session, so tmux becomes a hard dependency for any repository that declares a service.

## Also removes `TRACTOR_URL`

`.tractor/run` exported `PORT` and `TRACTOR_URL`. `TRACTOR_URL` should never have existed: it hardcodes HTTP, loopback, no base path, and that the address is a URL at all. The workflow decides what the port means.

The engine picks a free base port and passes `OVERMIND_PORT` and `--port-step`. Each process reads `$PORT` from its own environment. Nothing else is exported.

## Observability

Reading a process table on every node entry is what makes the state askable. The timeline gains an event per node entry naming which services were required and what state they were found in, and `tractor status` grows a services block:

```
services   overmind · Procfile · base port 55810
  web       pid 69685   running    required by implement, sprints
  worker    pid 69608   running    required by sprints
  checked   entering `sprints` at stage 11 — web accepted in 0.4s
```

## What this does not fix

A service that is only ever ensured *up* keeps serving whatever it booted with. `status` reports it running the whole time, because it is. A loop check at stage 12 then validates code nobody wrote — the false pass this whole area exists to prevent, arriving by a different road.

Restarting when the tree changes is what closes it, and that is deliberately out of scope here. This is a considered trade, not an oversight: the requirement primitive alone is already far better than 127 stages against nothing, and it is the smaller thing to build first. Workflows adopting this early should either have a Procfile process that builds before it serves, or a service that reads the tree live.

## Scope

Not building process orchestration. The engine holds an adapter over one manager and never supervises a process itself. If the six verbs above start growing, that is the signal to stop.

## Related

- #70 — supersedes it. The fix filed there was to export `TRACTOR_URL` into agent turns; the answer is instead that a required service is alive across the nodes that require it, and `TRACTOR_URL` goes away. Recommend closing #70 when this lands.
- #65 item 6 — the service scope question, answered here.
- #67 — an agent can repair `.tractor/run` mid-run. Moot once the file is gone, though the same hole exists for a Procfile.
- #60 — what this replaces.

title: Wake the host agent session when a run has news
body:
## Summary

An agent starts a Tractor run from inside a host agent session, then goes idle. The run keeps working, produces news, and nobody is listening. The agent only finds out when a human comes back and prompts it.

Tractor should be able to wake the session it was launched from and hand it a digest of what happened since the last wake.

The wake channel is host-specific. The digest is not: it is the same rollup a supervisor gets when it wakes to check the node it watches, which is #59.

## The wake channel is real and was verified for Claude Code

An external process on the same machine can push a turn into a running Claude Code session, including one that has already gone idle. This was tested end to end: a background session was started, allowed to finish its work and idle, then woken from a clean environment (`env -i`, no Claude tooling, `nc` only). It picked up the injected instruction and carried it out.

Two discovery paths:

- **Environment inheritance.** A Claude Code session exports `CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET` and `CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN`. A process it launches inherits both. This is the case that matters here: the agent runs `tractor start`, so Tractor already holds the coordinates of the session that started it.
- **Session registry.** `~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json` records `sessionId`, `cwd`, `messagingSocketPath`, `name`, and `kind`; a sibling `<pid>.<hash>.key` holds the auth token. This covers reattaching when the environment was not captured or was lost.

The protocol is two newline-delimited JSON frames over the Unix socket:

```
{"type":"auth","token":"<token>"}
{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":"<digest>"}}
```

The message frame shape matters. `{"type":"message","text":...}` is accepted by the socket and silently discarded — no error, no delivery. Only the `{"type":"user","message":{...}}` form is delivered.

### Guards to design around

Read out of the host implementation, not inferred:

- Per-sender token bucket, capacity 30, refill 0.5/sec. Sustained ceiling is one wake per two seconds, with a burst of 30.
- Identical message bodies from the same sender inside a 30-second window are dropped as duplicates. This is useful rather than harmful: a "nothing new" nudge suppresses itself. A digest with real content always differs.
- Messages are capped at 1 MB and error above it. This bounds whatever gets inlined.
- Hop-loop guards exist for session-to-session relay chains. Tractor sends no hop chain and is not subject to them.

Also present in the protocol, not exercised in the test: a `--messaging-socket-path` flag that lets a launcher dictate the socket path, and a `notify_idle` peer feature with a subscribe path — the primitive for learning that a session went idle instead of guessing.

## What Tractor needs

1. **Capture the host session at run start.** Whatever identifies the launching session goes into the run manifest so the detached runner can reach back. `runManifest` (`engine/control.go:19`) records nothing about its caller today. #71 is already expanding this struct for unrelated reasons; the two should agree on shape rather than collide.

2. **A waker.** Given captured host coordinates and a rendered digest, deliver it, respecting the host's rate and size limits, and degrade quietly when the session is gone. Nothing about a run should fail because a wake could not be delivered.

3. **A trigger policy.** The plausible triggers are: on specified events, after N agent turns, and on an interval. Which of these exist, and what the default is, is an open decision (see below).

4. **A digest.** Covered by #59.

## Relationship to #59

#59 is the same summary problem for supervisor patrols: `renderNudge` (`engine/supervisor.go:405`) hands the supervisor `live`, a `batch` path, a `count`, and a `tally`, so every patrol starts by opening files before any judgment happens. #59 is to inline the evidence instead.

A woken host session has the identical problem and pays more for it: the context spent reading files to discover whether anything is worth caring about is context taken from the user's own working session.

These should share one renderer — what happened since a cursor, inlined and bounded — with two consumers: supervisor patrols and host session wakes. #59 should land first or alongside; this issue should not grow its own second summary path.

Two constraints inherited from #59:

- #59 already names unbounded session growth: supervisor sessions are never compacted. A woken host session has the same exposure and it is the user's working session. Whatever bounding policy #59 settles on has to cover this consumer too.
- Every inlined section states whether it was truncated and where the full artifact lives.

## The cursor gap

"What happened since the last wake" needs a cursor, and the two candidate logs are not equally ready.

- `events/index.jsonl` carries a monotonic `seq` per line (`internal/runlog/allocator.go:70`). Clean to key on.
- `timeline.jsonl` is where the lifecycle events actually live and is stamped with `ts` but **has no sequence number** (`engine/store.go:96`). "Since X" there has to key on timestamp or byte offset.

The supervisor inbox sidesteps this entirely by rotating files on rename (`engine/supervisor.go:271`), which is a boundary rather than a cursor and does not generalise to a second consumer reading the same events.

Whether to add a sequence number to `timeline.jsonl` should be decided as part of this work rather than worked around.

## Doing the same thing for Codex

A run started from inside a Codex session has the same problem and should get the same behaviour. The digest half is host-agnostic and already shared. Only the channel differs.

Implementing the Codex side means answering, for Codex, the same questions that are answered above for Claude Code:

1. **Discovery.** What does a Codex session export into the environment of processes it launches that identifies the session or conversation? Is there a registry on disk — session, rollout, or thread files — that maps a discoverable id to something addressable?
2. **Transport.** What does an external process connect to? Tractor already speaks Codex's app-server JSON-RPC in `harness/codex/`, including `turn/steer` (`harness/codex/adapter.go:207`), but that is for conversations Tractor itself spawned over a stdio pipe it owns. The question is whether a conversation belonging to *another* process can be addressed, and over what. #20 asserts a local daemon exists and that the adapter wastefully ignores it; if that daemon is addressable by a second process, it is the obvious candidate. #10 covers generating the full wire protocol and would make the available methods explicit.
3. **Message shape.** Which method injects a user turn into an existing conversation, and what exactly does it accept. The Claude Code lesson applies: verify by observing delivery, not by the call returning without error.
4. **Idle behaviour.** Does injection wake a session that has already finished its turn, or only queue for a session still working? This is the whole point and must be tested against a genuinely idle session, not a busy one.
5. **Guards.** Rate limits, deduplication, size caps, and what happens when the target is gone.
6. **Idle notification.** Codex has a `notify` configuration hook that invokes an external program on events. If it reports a session going idle, that is a better wake trigger than an interval.

The shape to implement against: one interface with `capture` (record host coordinates at run start), `wake` (deliver a rendered digest), and `available` (is this host reachable). Claude Code is the reference implementation. Codex is a second implementation of the same interface, with the digest and trigger policy untouched.

Whoever takes the Codex half should treat every answer above as unverified until demonstrated against a live idle session, the way the Claude Code path was.

## Open decisions

These need a ruling and are not settled by this issue.

- **Triggers.** Which of on-event, after N turns, and on-interval exist, and which is the default. Waking on events is defensible. Waking a human's interactive session every thirty seconds will feel like an intruder.
- **Opt-in.** Whether waking is on by default for runs started from a host session, or requested explicitly at start.
- **Interactive sessions.** The verification above used a background session. Interactive sessions register the same inbox and are the ordinary target of the host's own session-to-session messaging, so the mechanism is the same, but injecting turns into a conversation a human is also using is a product question, not just a mechanical one.
- **Timeline sequence numbers.** Whether to add `seq` to `timeline.jsonl` or key the cursor on something else.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A run started from a host agent session records enough about that session to reach it later.
2. When the run has news, the launching session receives a digest without a human prompting it.
3. The digest is the same rollup a supervisor receives, from one shared renderer, bounded and truncation-labelled per #59.
4. Wake delivery respects the host's rate, deduplication, and size limits, and never fails a run when the session is unreachable or gone.
5. The wake path is behind an interface with at least one implementation proven against a genuinely idle session.
6. Trigger policy and default are documented and match whatever is ruled above.

title: chore: put the version back to 0.8.0
body:
The v0.9.0 tag and GitHub release were pulled. The four built-in workflows cannot complete a real loop — the reviewer has no way to reach the running application, and the only edge back to the loop asks it to declare the work "demonstrated", which it cannot honestly do. Confirmed by two live runs, 128 stages and 7 stages, neither of which changed a line of code.

`main` keeps the code. The version constants should not claim a release that does not exist.

title: fix(workflows): bound the agent cycle inside every loop body
body:
v0.9.0 shipped three workflows that could run forever.

`max_visits` sat on the loop node. A loop node is only reached when the body agrees the work is done — so a reviewer that keeps routing back to the coder never arrives at the node holding the budget. **The budget guarded the exit, not the treadmill.**

Observed in a real run: `sprint-execute` reached 128 stages — 64 implement turns, 63 review turns, and exactly **one** arrival at the loop node — and changed nothing. No validation ever ran, no service was ever started. The reviewer could not reach the running application (#70), so it correctly answered "not demonstrated" 63 times, and nothing stopped it.

`implement` and `review` in `sprint-execute` and `chapter-loop`, and `coding` and `review` in `delivery-loop`, now carry `max_visits: 12`. `resetVisits` fires when a new checklist item is selected, so the budget is per item rather than per run.

A test walks every built-in, takes each loop's body node-set via `lint.LoopBodyNodes`, and fails if any agent in it is unbounded. Verified by removing one budget and confirming the test fails.

**This bounds the damage; it does not fix the cause.** The reviewer still cannot reach the application — that is #70, and it is the actual bug.

title: docs: name the five arts of orchestration
body:
Tyler's framing, 2026-09-07, recorded as a live document rather than a settled one — he said himself he is not sure the dimensions are right.

Five competing priorities: making the agent actually do the work; splitting the work so no agent carries more than one can get right; helping the human define the work and author the workflow; showing humans and agents how the work is going; and letting observers steer it in flight.

The document also names the tensions, because they are the interesting part — every steering channel is a way to talk an agent into a verdict it should not reach, and checks written by the author of a plan tend to accommodate the plan.

Linked from AGENTS.md so agents read it before proposing features, and from the README for humans.

title: Run manifests do not record what was run: no argv, binary, pipeline source, or graph hash
body:
## The gap

A run directory cannot say what it ran. `manifest.json` records only:

```
control_socket  goal  id  name  started_at  workdir
```

There is no argv, no executable path or hash, no record of whether the pipeline came from a file or from the embedded catalogue, and no hash of the resolved graph.

## Why it matters

It makes run artifacts unusable as evidence. Adversarial review of the v0.9.0 verification runs landed on this as its strongest objection, and it is correct:

> The claimed inheritance proof is circular: the installed binary currently shows an inner loop with no checklist, while the run shows a resolved inner path — but the run never proves it used that embedded definition. A supplied graph with the path hardcoded would produce the same manifest, stages, prompts, validations, and ledgers.

So "I ran `tractor run chapter-loop` and it worked" is not checkable after the fact. Nothing distinguishes a run of the embedded workflow from a run of a local file, or from inline YAML, or from a copy since deleted. `name` in the manifest is the pipeline's own `name:` field, which any file can claim.

The same objection reappears for every claim a run directory is offered as evidence for, which is most of them.

## Fix

Record provenance in `manifest.json` at run start:

- `argv` as invoked
- the executable's path and, ideally, its build version
- how the pipeline was resolved: `builtin:<name>` or `file:<path>` or `inline`
- a hash of the resolved graph after parsing, so the manifest pins what actually ran rather than what was on disk at the time

None of it needs a schema change to the graph language, and all of it is known at the moment the run starts.

## Why now

This is the cheapest thing that makes proof artifacts self-evidencing, which is a prerequisite for gating releases on them (#69) and for treating a stored run as durable evidence at all. Without it, every proof needs a human to vouch for how it was produced.

## Related

Found by the adversarial review that also produced #70. Prerequisite for #69.

title: Agents start their own servers because only the item command gets TRACTOR_URL
body:
## The defect

The service lifecycle gives `PORT` and `TRACTOR_URL` to the checklist item's `command` and to nothing else. `engine/loop.go` passes `app.env()` into `runShell` for the item command only; every agent turn — implement, review, the `infer` judge, the goal evaluator — runs without them.

So an agent told to "run the software yourself; do not judge from the diff alone" has no way to reach the instance the engine started, and does the only thing it can: starts its own.

Observed across the v0.9.0 verification runs, in six stages. From a `chapter-loop` implement turn:

> Started the real server with `PORT=54321 go run ./cmd/server`, polled until it accepted connections, then ran the sprint's check command verbatim…

and the reviewer downstream then consumed that agent's narrative:

> the server process running from this workspace (pid 86333, listening on 127.0.0.1:54321) returns HTTP 200 with body "ok" on /health

## Why this matters more than it looks

This is the exact failure the service lifecycle exists to prevent, reintroduced one level up.

The engine allocates an unguessable port specifically so that nothing else can be mistaken for the build — then does not tell the agents, so they pick a memorable one. Two consequences:

1. **The verdict is about the wrong instance.** An agent's own server is built from the workspace at the moment the agent chose to start it, not the instance the engine started and validated. The reviewer's evidence describes a process the engine never knew about.
2. **Agent-started servers are not in the engine's process group**, so nothing tears them down. One that outlives its turn is listening on a guessable port for the next lap to find — which manufactures the stale-target case the design was built to eliminate.

No survivors were observed after these runs, so consequence 2 is a live hazard rather than an observed failure. Consequence 1 is observed.

## Fix

Export `PORT` and `TRACTOR_URL` into agent turns that run while a service is up, the same way the item command gets them, and say so in the prompts the built-in workflows use for their review nodes ("the running application is at `$TRACTOR_URL`").

That raises the scope question filed as item 6 of #65: today the service is started for the validation window only, so there is no instance alive during the implement and review turns to point at. Either the service window widens to cover the loop body, or the review nodes get their own window. The first is simpler and matches what the prompts already ask agents to do.

Whichever way that goes, an agent should never have to choose a port.

## How this was found

Adversarial review of the v0.9.0 verification runs, which was asked to attack the inference rather than confirm it. The runs themselves all completed and looked clean; the defect is only visible in what the agents wrote in their transcripts.

## Related

#65 item 6 filed this as a scope gap and understated it — this is not only a missing convenience for reviewers, it actively reintroduces the failure mode the feature was built to close. #67 is the neighbouring case where an agent repairs `.tractor/run`.
