title: Gate releases on live proof, using Tractor's own checklist validation
body:
## The problem

v0.9.0 shipped with a green test suite and nothing run end to end. The gap was noticed and written down as a footnote instead of stopping the release.

The `release-tractor` skill already covers this:

> Also run focused tests and live entry-point proof appropriate to the changed behavior. A passing test suite is not a substitute for exercising the released interface.

That is correct and it did not help, for two reasons. It sits in prose below a fenced block of commands, so the commands read as the gate and the sentence reads as advice. And it is only reached by loading the skill, which is exactly the step that gets skipped when a release is one item inside a larger request.

Prose that has to be remembered is not a gate.

## What live proof actually looks like here

Verified by hand after the fact. A scratch git repository with a deliberately broken HTTP server, a `.tractor/run`, and a checklist whose item curls the running service:

- `tractor run <pipeline>` — agent fixed the source, engine started the service on an allocated port, item command captured `status=200 body=ok`, judge passed, engine wrote `done: true`, run COMPLETED.
- Same repository with `.tractor/run` set to `exit 1` — item recorded `passed: false`, `infer: null`, `service never became ready`, no model consulted.
- `tractor run sprint-execute --goal ...` — the built-in resolved by name from the binary, walked `sprints → implement → review → sprints`, service on an allocated port, engine wrote `done`.

That is roughly twenty minutes and it caught a real defect the test suite could not (#67).

## Proposal

Gate the release on evidence rather than on remembering to gather it, using Tractor.

- A release checklist in the repository whose items carry the commands that produce this evidence: a scratch repository is built, a pipeline is run for real, and the item passes only when the engine wrote `done` and the run completed. The engine owns that, so a release cannot close on an assertion that it works.
- The `release-tractor` skill's publish step then depends on that checklist being closed, rather than on a sentence being remembered.
- The verification block in the skill should name the proof as a required artifact with a path, not as a closing paragraph.

The pleasing part is that this is what Tractor is for. If a checklist the engine validates is the right way to know a feature is done, it is the right way to know a release is releasable, and dogfooding it here costs one ledger.

## Open questions

- Which built-ins must be exercised per release: the ones whose files changed, or one representative every time? All four is expensive; `chapter-loop`, `sprint-plan` and `delivery-loop` are still unverified today.
- Whether the scratch repository is a committed fixture or built by the item's command each time. A fixture is faster and can go stale; building it each time is slower and always honest.

## Related

Discovered while closing out #65 and #67. Unverified as of now: `chapter-loop`, `sprint-plan`, `delivery-loop`.

title: An agent can repair .tractor/run mid-run and be validated against the repair
body:
## What happened

Found by running the software, not by reading it.

A loop was given a deliberately broken `.tractor/run` (`exit 1`) to prove that a service which never starts fails every item. It did, exactly as designed — stage 3 recorded `passed: false`, `infer: null`, and `service never became ready: .tractor/run exited before accepting on port 54810`, with no judge consulted.

Then the coding agent ran. Told to "change the source so the item's check is true", it repaired `.tractor/run` back to `exec go run ./cmd/server` along with the actual bug. The next lap started a service, validated against it, passed, and the engine marked the item done.

Every individual step was correct. The outcome is not.

## Why it matters

The engine owns `done` so that an agent cannot claim completion it did not earn. But the engine does not own **what gets started**, so an agent that cannot fake the verdict can change the subject instead — it rewrites the definition of the software being validated, and then the validation is honest about the wrong thing.

That is the same class of problem as an agent writing `done`, one level up. It is also the concrete instance of the environment-repair failure path: an agent with the repository in scope can fix the thing it is being judged against and then be judged against the fix.

Nothing was mis-implemented here. `.tractor/run` is an ordinary committed file and a coding agent legitimately has the repository. The gap is that nothing marks it as the one file whose meaning the run depends on.

## Options

- **Snapshot at run start.** The engine reads `.tractor/run` once when the run begins and uses that for the whole run, so mid-run edits do not change what is validated. Cheap, no schema change, and mirrors how `done` is taken out of an agent's hands. Changing how the app starts then requires a new run, which seems right.
- **Detect and surface.** Hash it at start, compare on each arrival, and record a timeline event when it changed. Weaker, but keeps a legitimate mid-run fix possible while making it visible.
- **Put it out of reach.** Once agent turns get an isolated workdir (#65, item 1), a validating turn cannot touch it at all — but a *coding* turn still can, and should be able to, so this does not fully solve it.

Snapshot-at-start looks right and is the smallest. Flagging rather than deciding: whether a mid-run change to how the application starts should be impossible or merely visible is a judgement call.

## Evidence

Live run, four stages, in a scratch repository with a deliberately broken health endpoint and a deliberately broken service file:

- stage `000003-work` — service down, item failed, `infer: null`, no model consulted
- stage `000004-fix` — agent repaired both `cmd/server/main.go` and `.tractor/run`
- stage `000005-work` — service up on port 54914, item passed, engine wrote `done: true`

## Related

Part of the validation cleanup in #65; the isolation work there (item 1) is adjacent but does not close this on its own.

title: Serve the graph editor through skgo

The editor page behind `tractor edit` is now a SvelteKit 3 app on the vite-plus stack, built by the skgo adapter and embedded from `web/editor/build`. title: Make validation fluent: isolation, artifacts, a validation node, and declared arguments
body:
## Purpose

Validation is the thing Tractor exists to get right, and it is currently assembled by hand out of parts that do not know about each other. A checklist item's `command` and `infer` are the right shape — the engine owns `done`, a judge reads evidence, a failing item reopens — but authoring that well is hard enough that pipelines reach for a test command instead, and several structural holes let a validator reach a verdict it did not earn.

This issue collects the whole topic: what landed in v0.9.0, what is still missing, one open design question, and the rule that keeps it from turning into a process orchestrator.

**The dichotomy this is answering, in Tyler's words:** unit tests, linters and tripwires are wanted everywhere and are good for code quality, algorithms and edge cases — *and they are not proof of work*. A check in the loop is fine. What is missing is a validator that has no stake in completion, cannot see the source, understands that pass/fail is whether the application satisfies its promises rather than a hunt for hypothetical bugs, and **cannot report success except insofar as it actually saw the software working**.

The strongest form of that last requirement which an engine can actually enforce: *no pass unless the engine started the application, observed it become ready, and the verdict was adjudicated only from artifacts produced inside that window.* Everything beyond that is prompt discipline and should be recognised as such.

## Landed in v0.9.0 (#60)

`.tractor/run` — the engine allocates a port, exports `PORT` and `TRACTOR_URL`, starts the repository's own command in a process group, waits for the port to accept, validates the whole set against that one instance, then signals the group away. An application that never accepts fails every item with no judge consulted.

That closes the worst false pass: a validator that truthfully observed the wrong thing — a stale server from the last lap, a developer's own instance, a staging URL. Nothing downstream can catch that, because the evidence is authentic. It is closed by the port being unguessable, not by instruction.

## Open work

### 1. Turn isolation and declared artifacts

Every LLM turn opens with `WithCwd(workdir)` and `PermissionModeBypassAll` (`harness/claude/native.go:25`), and `AgentNode` has no workdir field. That applies to the `infer` judge and to the goal evaluator, whose prompt tells it to "open and inspect every file" (`engine/loop.go`).

So a validator has a shell in the repository. It can read the implementer's commits, and — worse — repair the environment it was sent to judge and then approve its own repair. Source-blindness alone does not close this; taking the working directory away closes all three at once.

- `workdir` or `isolated: true` on agent nodes and on the judge, so the turn's cwd is a scratch directory holding the task and an empty evidence directory.
- Declared `artifacts`, collected the way `fan_out` branch artifacts already are (`engine/artifacts.go`), with zero artifacts a hard failure. `infer` already fails on zero matched evidence files (`engine/loop.go:330`); this generalises that.
- The judge must not receive the validator's prose. If it can read "I signed in successfully" it is the same claim laundered through a second model; isolation is only real when the judge's input differs in kind from the actor's output.

### 2. A validation node — open design question

**Tyler's proposal (not yet ruled on):** a node dedicated to validation, possibly a new kind of supervisor. It patrols on its own clock, gets application rebuilds on node transitions, and when it detects that the application validates, marks the thing done so the development loop can exit — "like an async synchronization primitive."

**The counter-argument (Claude and a Fable reviewer, not ratified):** Tractor's node types each carry routing semantics — loop owns `done`, supervisor cannot route, command routes on exit code — and a `validation` type may add none that an `agent` node with an enforced contract does not already have. And a type hardcoded to a browser ages badly: CLIs, HTTP services and daemons are the same problem with a different client.

Both readings survive the discussion and this is Tyler's call. Note the async design needs item 3 before it is sound, or it is a race: it can pass against a commit that no longer exists and release the loop on a stale verdict.

### 3. Verdicts that record what they were taken against

`done: true` says an item passed, not what it passed against. Re-attestation runs on every lap inside a run and stops when the run does, so a ledger committed with every box ticked is a claim about a moment that has passed.

Stamping a verdict with the commit it was taken at, and only releasing on a verdict whose commit is HEAD, is both the fix for the async validator above and the answer to what a checked box means.

**#51 trials exactly this at workflow level, and Tyler accepted that framing explicitly as not a core feature.** Anything here should wait on what that trial shows rather than pre-empt it.

### 4. Declared run arguments

`--goal` is a literal `strings.ReplaceAll` of `$goal` and is the entire input interface. Nothing can carry a fact a run needs.

- `args:` on the pipeline as a flat JSON Schema, validated at startup and refusing to launch on violation, the way the graph is already linted before a token burns.
- `$args.k` substituted in prompts. `$goal` becomes `args.goal`, required by default, `--goal` kept as UX; `NeedsGoal` in the workflow catalogue becomes schema `required`, which removes a special case rather than adding a system.
- Hard limits, or this becomes a template language: flat scalars only, non-scalars refused at lint, no conditionals or expressions.
- An argument substituted into a `command` string is shell — quote it or refuse it.
- Secrets do not go here. A seeded password would land in prompts, run logs and the timeline. Environment, not arguments.
- **Facts the engine consumes are not arguments.** How the application starts and what port it listens on belong in `.tractor/run`. A base URL in prompt text is how a validator picks its own target again.

### 5. Loops cannot say they need a service

The presence of `.tractor/run` is the entire opt-in, so `tractor validate` cannot tell you a workflow that needs an application has no way to start one — you find out on the first lap. A field on the loop node would let lint catch it, at the cost of a schema change. Deliberately deferred in #60.

### 6. Where the service is available

The service is up for validation only. A reviewing agent that wants to use the application does not get one, which is a real gap for the "run the software yourself rather than reading the diff" review nodes in the built-in workflows.

### 7. Re-attestation cost

The engine re-validates every done item on every arrival. With browser validators that is every scenario, every lap, up to the loop's budget. Starting the application once per arrival (already done) is the main mitigation, but the cost is still linear in closed items and will be felt first here.

### 8. Criteria that cannot drift toward what got built

`df-easy-loop-e2e` upstream fixes acceptance criteria during the requirements interview, before code exists, and fails validation if any is unmet regardless of what else passed.

**Tyler's ruling:** a holdout set is overrated as redundancy. Forcing an independent agent to actually use fully-built software beats it, and plotting quasi-random paths through an application yields more than a fixed list ever will. A holdout earns its place specifically where there is a table of data and the application must behave predictably across all the tuples — that is a designer's call about the shape of the promise.

What survives is not the *holdout* but the *fixed*: criteria should be shown to the implementer, and must not be editable downstream to match what got built. Related: in `delivery-loop` the `plan` node writes both the plan and its checks, so the checks inherit the planner's stake — they likely belong to `plan_critique`, which already asks where an item's check would pass while the item is false.

## The rule that keeps this bounded

**Tractor holds one handle and never looks inside it.** It knows a PID, a port and an exit status — not how many processes there are, what they are, or what order they start in. `exec go run ./cmd/server`, `OVERMIND_PORT=$PORT exec overmind start` and `exec docker compose up` are indistinguishable from the engine's side.

The test for any field proposed here: *does it require the engine to know something about the inside of the handle?* If so it does not belong. That is why there is no `ready:`, `env:`, `depends_on:`, `services:`, `build:` or `port:` — each is a step toward reimplementing Compose badly, and there are better implementations of that than we will ever write.

## Known residual, not planned

Allocating a port means bind-close-reuse, which is a TOCTOU race. It is closed in practice by watching the child: an application that cannot bind almost always exits, and an exit before readiness draws a fresh port and retries. What remains needs an application to fail to bind, survive anyway, *and* an unrelated HTTP server to occupy that exact ephemeral port. Closing it would mean asking the OS which PID holds the listener — `/proc/net/tcp` on Linux, `lsof` on macOS, no Go stdlib. Recorded rather than pretended away; not worth the platform code until it bites.

## Related

#56 per-node skills, #58 model role presets, #59 supervisor nudge content, #51 stale-revision review trial, #48 bounded validation log reads.

title: Start the software under test, on a port the engine picks
body:
Closes the false pass that evidence review cannot catch.

## The hole

The dangerous false positive in agentic validation is not a lying validator. It is a truthful one pointed somewhere else — a stale dev server from the previous lap, a developer's own instance on the usual port, a staging URL. The browser really drove it, the screenshots are real, the application really works. It is just not the code under test, and nothing downstream can detect that, because the evidence is authentic.

Nothing could start the application, so whoever validated it had to. `runShell` puts every command in its own process group and kills it on return, so no node can leave a server running.

## `.tractor/run`

A repository says how it starts, once, in a committed file. The contents go to `/bin/sh`, the same as any command node.

```sh
exec go run ./cmd/server
```

On each loop arrival the engine allocates a free port, exports `PORT` and `TRACTOR_URL`, runs the file in its own process group, and waits for the port to accept before validating anything. Every item in the set is validated against that one instance — one start per arrival, not one per item, which is what keeps a browser validator affordable across a long loop. The group is signalled away afterwards: SIGTERM first, so a supervisor like `docker compose up` tears its own children down rather than leaking containers, then SIGKILL after a grace period so nothing survives to become the next lap's target.

**Picking the port is the guarantee, not a convenience.** A stale server, a developer's instance, and staging are all somewhere else by construction. Nothing can be sitting on a port nobody could have guessed.

## Not being a process supervisor

Tractor holds one handle and never looks inside it. It knows a PID, a port, and an exit status — not how many processes there are, what they are, or what order they start in. `exec go run ./cmd/server`, `OVERMIND_PORT=$PORT exec overmind start`, and `exec docker compose up` are indistinguishable from here, and everything a process supervisor does stays inside the handle where the engine cannot see it. That is the test for any future field: does it require knowing something about the inside? If so, it does not belong.

So there is no `ready:`, `env:`, `depends_on:`, `services:`, `build:`, or `port:`. Each is a step toward reimplementing Compose badly. The port accepting is the readiness probe, and a port you chose is a port something else can already be sitting on. A tool with its own spelling is adapted in the file itself.

## Not ready is a failure

An application that never accepts fails every item in the set, **with no judge consulted and no agent turn taken**. Inability to observe is a failure, never an absence of findings, and there is no inconclusive verdict for a model to reach for. The service log tail lands in the validation record so the reason is in front of whoever reads the run.

## The port race

Bind-close-reuse is a real TOCTOU: between the engine's `Close()` and the application's `bind()` — seconds, for anything with a startup — something else can take the port. It is closed by watching the child. An application that cannot bind almost always exits, and an exit before readiness draws a fresh port and tries once more.

What that leaves is an application that fails to bind, survives anyway, *and* an unrelated HTTP server occupying that exact ephemeral port. Closing that too would mean asking the OS which PID holds the listener — `/proc/net/tcp` on Linux, `lsof` on macOS, no Go stdlib. Not worth it until it bites; noted rather than pretended away.

## Tests

`TestLoopValidatesAgainstTheApplicationTheEngineStarted` is the end-to-end: a repository with a `.tractor/run`, a checklist whose item command reads `$TRACTOR_URL`, and an assertion that the engine marked it done. The command would fail without the service, so it is a real assertion rather than a smoke test.

`TestLoopFailsEveryItemWhenTheApplicationNeverStarts` uses an item command that would pass on its own (`true`) and asserts it stays open, because there was nothing to observe.

Alongside those: the port is bindable after allocation, stop releases it, stop is idempotent, a readiness failure carries the service's own stderr, and an operator stop reaches the readiness wait.

## Follow-ups, not in this change

- `tractor validate` cannot say a service file is missing, because a loop does not declare that it needs one — the file's presence is the whole opt-in. A `service: true` on the loop node would let lint catch it, at the cost of a schema change.
- The service is up for validation only. A reviewing agent that wants to use the application does not get it yet.
- A verdict does not record the commit it was taken at, which is what an asynchronous validator would need before it could release a loop.

title: Give supervisors their evidence in the nudge instead of a path to it
body:
## Summary

Put what the supervisor needs into the patrol nudge, instead of handing it paths and making it go looking.

## What a patrol looks like today

`renderNudge` in `engine/supervisor.go` builds the message from four things:

- `live` — the in-scope live executions, each `{node_id, attempt, run_log}`, where `run_log` is a path
- `batch` — a path to the rotated inbox file, `inbox.NNNNNN.jsonl`
- `count` — how many digests are in that batch
- `tally` — per-node disposition counts

The digests themselves are the interesting part and they are not in the message. `attemptDigest` already carries the node, disposition, attempt, stage directory, chosen next node, notes, error category, and message; `supervisorDigest` carries verdicts and coaching. All of it is written to the inbox file, and the supervisor receives the filename.

So every patrol begins with the supervisor opening files to find out what happened. To answer anything about the substance of the work — whether a change serves the requirement, whether an agent is building proof machinery instead of running the software — it has to go further and read the stage directory or the diff itself.

Two things make this more wasteful than it looks:

- The supervisor sees only paths, so the cheapest possible patrol still costs a round of tool calls before any judgment starts.
- The judgment is narrow and repeats on a clock for the length of the run, so the overhead is paid tens of times per supervised node.

## What is already in place

The session is not fresh each patrol. `prepareSupervisorBinding` mints the native session once per supervisor node and reuses it, which is why the briefing is sent once and marked idempotent. The supervisor accumulates history across patrols.

That matters for the design: the nudge should carry the delta, not the whole state. The inbox rotation is already delta-shaped — each batch is what happened since the last flush.

## Proposal

1. Inline the rotated batch's digests in the nudge rather than naming the file. They are small, structured, and already exactly what the supervisor wants. Keep the path as well, for the cases where it wants more than was inlined.
2. Include a bounded summary of what changed in the workspace since the last patrol — name-status plus a size-capped patch, with the full diff left on disk. The engine already knows the git workspace; making each supervisor shell out for this repeatedly is duplicated work.
3. Keep both bounded and say so in the nudge, so the supervisor knows when it is looking at a truncation and can go read the rest.

## The constraint this runs into

Supervisor sessions are never compacted. `prepareBinding` handles fidelity and calls `adapter.Compact` for `FidelityCompacted`; `prepareSupervisorBinding` has no fidelity handling at all. A supervisor's session therefore grows for the whole run.

That is survivable while the nudge is four small fields. It stops being survivable once diffs are being inlined every few minutes for hours. So this issue needs one of:

- a compaction policy for supervisor sessions, or
- a rotation policy that starts a fresh supervisor session periodically and re-sends the briefing, or
- hard caps on inlined content tight enough that growth stays bounded across a long run.

Whichever is chosen should be decided as part of this change rather than after it.

## The second consumer: the woken host session

This renderer has two consumers, not one, and the second one already exists.
#75 has landed: a run started from inside an agent session wakes that session
on an interval and hands it a rollup of what happened since the last wake. It
ships with a deliberately thin interim renderer in `engine/wake.go` (`render`),
written to be deleted. This issue is what replaces it, and the two consumers
should be served at the same time rather than one after the other.

What that adds to the work here:

- **Scope is a parameter, not a constant.** A supervisor asks for its own
  `supervises` scope. A woken host session asks for the whole run: it started
  the run, not one node, and nothing narrows it. Same renderer, same sections,
  a scope argument that is either a node set or the run.
- **The delta boundary differs.** A supervisor's delta is the rotated inbox
  batch. A host wake's delta is everything on `timeline.jsonl` since the last
  delivered `HostWake` event, which is the cursor #75 established. The renderer
  takes the events it is given; each consumer decides what "since" means.
- **The bounding policy has to cover both.** The constraint above names
  supervisor sessions growing for the whole run. A woken host session has the
  same exposure and a worse version of it: it is the user's own working
  session, and every byte inlined is context taken from the work they are
  doing. Whichever policy is chosen has to be stated for this consumer too, and
  the host caps a delivered message at a megabyte, which is far larger than
  anything either consumer should receive.
- **Truncation labelling is already load-bearing.** #75 delivers bounded,
  truncation-labelled sections today because a woken session that cannot tell
  a truncation from the whole story will act on half a picture. Criterion 3
  below is what the wake path is already keeping; it should not regress when
  the shared renderer takes over.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A patrol nudge contains the digests from its batch, not only the batch path.
2. A patrol nudge contains a bounded summary of workspace change since the previous patrol.
3. Every inlined section states whether it was truncated and where the full artifact lives.
4. Supervisor session growth across a long run is bounded by an explicit, documented policy.
5. A supervisor that reads nothing at all can still return a useful verdict on ordinary patrols.
6. The renderer serves both consumers from one path: supervisor patrols scoped to `supervises`, and the host session woken by #75 scoped to the whole run.
7. The bounding policy in criterion 4 is stated for the woken host session as well, and `engine/wake.go`'s interim renderer is gone.

title: Runtime-configurable model presets: name the role, not the model
body:
## Summary

Let a node name a role rather than a model, and let the operator decide what each role resolves to at runtime.

```yaml
presets:
  manager: fable
  workhorse: claude-sonnet-5
  heavy: claude-opus-5
  validation: gpt
  evidence: flash
```

```yaml
- id: implement
  type: agent
  model: workhorse
```

## Why

**The same mapping is retyped in every file.** The five workflows in `examples/workflows/` use four roles between them — a manager for planning and for every loop's goal evaluator, a workhorse for ordinary turns, a validator that always runs on the other provider from the coder, and a cheap judge for evidence. That convention is currently spelled out node by node in five files. Changing the workhorse means editing every node that has one.

**Roles are stable; models are not.** A pipeline that says `claude-sonnet-5` is stale the next time the family moves. A pipeline that says `workhorse` is not.

**Operators differ.** Someone without Codex access, someone who wants the heavy model everywhere, someone running as cheaply as possible, and CI all want the same graph with different models. Today the only way to get that is to fork the file.

**The engine already thinks in roles.** `engine/model_selection.go` has `RoleItemJudge` and `RoleGoalEvaluator` with their own system defaults, and `tractor inspect-models` already prints every effective selection with its source. Presets generalize a mechanism that exists rather than adding a parallel one.

## Alias gap

`gpt`, `flash`, and `fable` are maintained aliases. There is no `opus` or `sonnet`, so the workhorse role cannot be named without a provider-native ID — `claude-sonnet-5` or `claude-opus-5` spelled out. Worth adding those aliases regardless of whether presets land, since a preset table wants short names on both sides.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A node's `model` may name a preset instead of a model selection, and the two forms are distinguishable at parse time.
2. Presets resolve from operator configuration, and a pipeline may override any of them in its defaults for the cases where the graph genuinely requires a specific model.
3. `tractor inspect-models` reports the preset name alongside what it resolved to and where that resolution came from, the way it already reports selection sources.
4. An unknown preset name is a lint error at `start_run`, not a fallback to a default.
5. The existing internal roles resolve through the same table, so the item judge and goal evaluator are configurable the same way as everything else.
6. Pipelines that name models directly keep working unchanged.
7. A run records the resolved model for every node in its manifest, so a run stays readable after the operator's preset table changes.

## Note

This pairs with #56. Skills make a node's instructions portable; presets make its model portable. Between them a pipeline file stops encoding one machine's setup.

title: Ship four workflows in the binary, ported from the diffusioninc skills
body:
Mounts the diffusioninc skills as a read-only reference submodule, and ships four workflows ported from them inside the binary.

## The submodule

`reference/diffusion-skills` tracks github.com/diffusioninc/skills. Read-only is a policy, not a git feature, so it is backed by three things: `ignore = dirty` in `.gitmodules` so edits inside the mirror never reach status or the index, a push URL pointed at a dead scheme in each clone, and the policy written down in `reference/README.md` and `AGENTS.md`. CI does not check out submodules, so the build is untouched.

## The workflows

Four pipelines embedded from `internal/workflows/`, each run by name. A catalogue beside them supplies the line the listing prints, and a test holds the catalogue and the files to each other, so a workflow cannot ship undocumented or be documented without shipping. Diagrams rendered from the files themselves with `tractor edit`.

```
$ tractor workflows
sprint-execute  Work a planned sprint ledger to done, one sprint per lap, each demonstrated…  needs docs/sprints/ledger.md
chapter-loop    Carry a chapter's worth of work in one run: chapters holding sprints holding…  needs docs/chapters/ledger.md
sprint-plan     Plan the next sprint properly: three independent drafts, mutual critique, you…  needs --goal
delivery-loop   Turn a written specification into working software while you are away.          needs --goal
```

The third column is what a workflow wants before it will do anything. A workflow either works on whatever you name and refuses to start without a `--goal`, or reads a file the workspace must already hold — named there, so a missing ledger is a stated precondition rather than a surprise on the first node.

`--goal` is new on `tractor run` and replaces the pipeline's goal, so every `$goal` a prompt expands is yours. Embedding the pipelines is what made this necessary: an example is parameterized by copying it and editing the goal, and a built-in cannot be. The two that need a goal refuse to start without one rather than running against the generic goal in their file, and the listing marks them.

`tractor workflows show <name>` prints a pipeline verbatim, so redirecting it into a file is how you adapt one. Every command that takes a pipeline now takes a built-in name as well — `tractor run sprint-execute`, `tractor validate sprint-execute`. A file on disk always wins, so a local pipeline is never shadowed by one in the binary.

Advertised on the front page, in `llms.txt`, in the tractor skill's moment table, and on a new docs page.

The upstream skills are pipeline engines written as prose — one of them embeds a YAML workflow definition and then spends two hundred lines instructing a model to be that runtime by hand. The engine already is that runtime, so the port is mostly deletion: preflight CLI checks, backgrounded shells and `wait`, outcome files for routing, and the protocol about which agent may check a plan box all disappear into things Tractor already does.

### Supervisors

Three, each named by the question it asks, patrolling outside the walk and steering one named target at a time.

They run on the workhorse tier, not the manager tier: the judgment is narrow — is this in the requirement or not — and it repeats on a clock for the length of the run, every 180s. A supervisor keeps one native session throughout, so it is not re-deriving state each patrol; what it pays for is being handed paths rather than content, which is #59.

**`serves_the_requirement`** watches the coding and validating agents for work nobody asked for: speculative fixes, hardening against conditions the requirement never mentions, edge cases outside the stated outcome, a second mechanism where one already works.

**`proof_is_evidence`** watches the validating agents for proof becoming a project of its own. Proof means running the software and recording what happened — not exhaustive coverage, not a harness that anticipates every input, not a reason to invent requirements the work never promised so they can be tested. The steer is always toward the concrete: run the thing, capture the output or the screenshot, say whether it worked.

**`done_is_demonstrable`** watches the planners for definitions of done that are lists of commands. `go test ./...`, `golangci-lint run ./...`, `lefthook run pre-commit` say nothing about whether the feature exists. "Build the feature described in the goal document, write the scenarios in Gherkin, implement them, demonstrate the feature in a real browser, then collect screenshots and look at them" says what done looks like and leaves the route to the implementer.

### Model roles

Four roles recur across all four, so the choices follow one convention rather than being decided node by node: **manager** for the planner, the merge, and every loop's goal evaluator (`fable`); **workhorse** for ordinary turns (`claude-sonnet-5`, raised to `claude-opus-5` where a node reasons over a whole codebase); **validation** for the reviewer, always on the other provider from whoever wrote the code (`gpt`); and **evidence** for the item judge over screenshots and artifacts (the engine's own gemini flash default).

The convention is retyped in every file, and the workhorse cannot be named briefly at all — `gpt`, `flash`, and `fable` are maintained aliases, while sonnet and opus have to be spelled as provider-native IDs. #58 is the fix.

### sprint-execute

The sprint ledger is the checklist; each item carries the command that demonstrates that sprint. The reviewer runs on the other provider with fresh context and cannot route to success — leaving the loop is the loop node's decision against the ledger's definition of done.

![sprint-execute](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tylergannon/tractor/main/ephemeral/projects/tractor/workflows/diagrams/sprint-execute.png)

### chapter-loop

The same shape nested. A chapter item names its own sprint ledger, the inner loop iterates it, the coding and validation loop sits inside that. One run, no child runs per chapter. A chapter's proof is its item's command and infer judge, so the chapter exit gate lands where the engine already owns done.

![chapter-loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tylergannon/tractor/main/ephemeral/projects/tractor/workflows/diagrams/chapter-loop.png)

### sprint-plan

Three providers draft the same intent in isolated worktrees, then each critiques the two drafts it did not write. The interview is a real gate: one node writes the questions, a command node blocks on `tractor ask` until the answers appear, the merge reads them. Drop those two nodes for an unattended plan.

![sprint-plan](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tylergannon/tractor/main/ephemeral/projects/tractor/workflows/diagrams/sprint-plan.png)

### delivery-loop

Plan, cross-provider critique, plan update, then a loop over the plan's own checklist. Writing the plan as a checklist file is what removes the upstream protocol where only the review agent may check boxes: the engine validates each item and flips done itself.

![delivery-loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tylergannon/tractor/main/ephemeral/projects/tractor/workflows/diagrams/delivery-loop.png)

## Second pass

A review of the shipped set found four defects, fixed in 7cabeee.

`sprint-execute` and `chapter-loop` each ran `go test ./...` between implement and review. That locked a general-purpose built-in to Go, and in any other repository the gate failed every lap and routed back to implement until the budget ran out. It was also redundant: the ledger item already carries the command that demonstrates it, and the loop node runs that on arrival. Both test nodes are gone, and no built-in hardcodes a test command now.

`sprint-plan`'s ledger entry is the handoff to `sprint-execute`, and nothing said the checklist shape that workflow requires. The merge prompt now names it.

`sprint-plan`'s questions → ask → error → questions cycle had no budget. `questions` now carries `max_visits`.

`promise-loop` invoked a `promise` executable that exists nowhere — upstream it is a script bundled inside a skill. A workflow that cannot run is worse than no workflow, so it is removed rather than shipped as a shape. What it was reaching for is mostly already here: the checklist is the contract, items are gates, `command` and `infer` are its two verifier kinds, and the engine already reopens a done item that stops passing. What is missing is that `done` does not record what it was proven against.

## Related

All four would rather declare their doctrine as skills than carry it in prompts, which is #56. All four would rather name model roles than model IDs, which is #58. Both were filed from this reading.

## Status

They ship, they lint, and the CLI serves them. None of the four has been run end to end yet, and the docs say so.

title: Per-node skills: declare skills on a workflow step, resolved and scoped by the engine
body:
## Summary

Let a workflow step declare the skills it needs, by name, path, or GitHub URL. The engine resolves them, pins them, and puts them in scope for that node only. Some skills ship inside the binary; the rest are downloaded and cached.

```yaml
- id: implement
  type: agent
  skills:
    - tractor:sprint-execute
    - ./team-skills/house-style
    - github.com/diffusioninc/skills@d0cdcd6#.claude/skills/df-sprint-plan
  prompt: $goal
```

## Why

Two reasons, and the second is the urgent one.

**Doctrine belongs in skills, not in prompts.** The workflows worth building — a sprint loop, a chapter loop, a promise loop — are small graphs wrapped around a lot of prose about how the work is done. Today that prose has to be pasted into node prompts, which makes it unversionable, unshareable, and impossible to reuse across pipelines. As a skill it travels on its own, and the graph goes back to being control flow.

**Skills already leak into runs, undeclared.** Tractor never sets `SkillsConfig`, so the Claude SDK defaults apply (`EnableSkills: true`, `SettingSources: ["user", "project"]`) and the transport emits `--setting-sources user,project`. Every Claude node in every run today loads whatever is installed in the operator's `~/.claude/skills` and in the workdir's `.claude/skills`. Nothing about that appears in the pipeline file, nothing is pinned, and two machines can run the same graph differently. A pipeline is supposed to be the whole story of a run. Declaring skills per node is also how that gets closed: a node with no `skills` field should load none.

## Mechanisms

Both real harnesses already have a per-turn hook.

**Claude.** The CLI accepts `--plugin-dir` and `--plugin-dir-no-mcp`; a plugin directory is a directory with `skills/` in it. The adapter already passes arbitrary flags through `WithExtraArgs` (`harness/claude/native.go`, used for `json-schema` and `session-id`), and opens a fresh client per turn (`harness/claude/adapter.go`, `runNativeTurn`), so `nativeConfig` is already the per-turn place to put this. No SDK change needed. Prefer `--plugin-dir-no-mcp` so a fetched bundle cannot introduce MCP servers.

**Codex.** The app-server turn input has a native skill element: `SkillUserInput {type: "skill", name, path}` in `harness/codex/schema/TurnStartParams.json`. Turn input is built in `nativeInput` (`harness/codex/adapter.go`), which today emits text parts only. Attaching a skill to a single turn is a change to that one function.

**agy.** No skill surface; the adapter passes `-p`, `--add-dir`, model, effort, and schema.

So the portable floor is a frame. `engine/frames.go` already injects engine-rendered blocks ahead of codergen and fan-in prompts. A skills frame listing each skill's name, description, and path — body left on disk for the agent to read — works on every harness including agy, and is the same progressive disclosure the native mechanisms use. Native attachment is then a per-harness optimization, not a prerequisite.

## Shape

Add `skills` to `LLMNodeFields` so agent, fan-in, and loop roles all get it, and to pipeline `defaults`.

Three source forms:

- `tractor:<name>` — bundled in the binary via `embed.FS`
- a local path — relative to the pipeline file
- `<host>/<owner>/<repo>@<ref>#<subdir>` — fetched with a shallow clone, `<subdir>` optional

One resolver in `internal/skills`: resolve, cache under a shared root keyed by resolved commit, materialize a per-node directory in the run directory by symlink. All three forms land in the same cache so one code path materializes them.

Resolution happens during the `start_run` lint pass. An unknown skill name, a missing path, an unreachable repository, or a missing subdirectory fails the run before a token burns, the same as any other graph error.

## Pinning

A ref resolves to a commit at lint time and the commit goes in the run manifest. An unpinned source should be a lint error, not a warning. These bundles ship executable scripts, and the agent that reads them runs with permissions bypassed, so an unpinned URL is remote code execution against the operator's machine. The resolved commit is also what makes a run reproducible.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `skills` is a typed, optional field on agent, fan-in, and loop-role nodes, and on pipeline defaults. Unknown fields inside it are parse errors like everywhere else.
2. The three source forms resolve: bundled, local path, and repository URL with optional subdirectory and required ref.
3. Resolution and materialization happen at lint time; every failure mode above stops the run before it starts.
4. A resolved skill set is recorded in the run manifest with the commit each source resolved to.
5. A Claude node receives its skills through a per-node plugin directory and no others; a node with no `skills` field loads no skills, including none from `~/.claude/skills` or the workdir.
6. A Codex node receives its skills as skill inputs on its own turns.
7. An agy node, and any node whose harness has no native mechanism, receives a skills frame naming each skill and its path.
8. Skills declared on a loop role apply on every lap without re-fetching.
9. At least one skill ships in the binary and is reachable as `tractor:<name>` with no network.

## Slices

1. Bundled skills, local paths, the frame fallback, and the Claude plugin directory. Useful on its own and needs no network.
2. The repository fetcher: resolver, cache, pinning, lint-time failures, manifest record.
3. Codex native skill inputs.

## Note

The upstream bundles this is modelled on keep two byte-mirrored copies of every skill, one for Claude and one for other runtimes, with a validation script enforcing parity. That duplication exists only because there is no common runtime. If the engine materializes per-node skill directories itself, it reads one bundle and presents it in whichever shape each harness wants, and the mirror problem does not reach anyone running through Tractor.
